The scope includes combination products which, for purposes of this guideline, may contain a scheduled substance, medicine, and/or a medical device. This guideline does not include products that are, for example, regulated under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies 1 WHO QAS/16.664, 2026. and Stock Remedies Act, 1947 (Act 36 of 1947). 2. LEGAL PROVISIONS According to Section 2A of the Medicines Act, the objects of SAHPRA are to monitor, evaluate, regulate, investigate, inspect, register, and control medicines, scheduled substances, clinical trials, medical devices, including in-vitro diagnostics (IVDs), and related matters in the public interest. The legal definitions of a “medicine, medical device, and a scheduled substance” are provided in Section 1 of the same Act, while Section 15 provides for the registration of medicines, medical devices, and IVDs. If SAHPRA is satisfied that a medicine or medical device should be registered in terms of section 15(3)(a) of the Medicines Act, SAHPRA may register the medicine or medical device subject to conditions determined in terms of section 15(6). Before embarking on the process of application for registration of a product, a decision may, however, be needed as to whether the product in question does indeed fall within the ambit of the Medicines Act. This guideline has been developed to guide that decision-making process. It must be noted, however, that products regulated under both the Medicines Act and the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act may in addition to specific regulatory control under these Acts,

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: does indeed fall within the ambit of the Medicines Act. This guideline has been developed to guide that decision-making process. It must be noted, however, that products regulated under both the Medicines Act and the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act may in addition to specific regulatory control under these Acts, also be regulated by aspects of other legislation including but not limited to: • the National Health Act, 2003 (Act 61 of 2003); • the Hazardous Substances Act, 1973 (Act 15 of 1973); • the National Regulator for Compulsory Specification Act, 2008 (Act 4 of 2008); or • the Legal Metrology Act, 2014 (Act 9 of 2014). In addition, all products which fall under the definition of ‘goods’ as defined in the Consumer Protection Act 2008 (Act 68 of 2008) are also regulated by that Act. 3. HEALTH PRODUCTS Medicine A medicine is defined in the Medicine Act as: “(a) any substance or mixture of substances used or purporting to be suitable for use or manufactured or sold for use in— (i) the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, modification, or prevention of disease, abnormal physical or mental state or the symptoms thereof in humans; or (ii) restoring, correcting, or modifying any somatic or psychic, or organic function in humans, and (b) includes any veterinary medicine.” A substance or mixture of substances may be classified as a medicine based on what it is used for, or is claimed to be suitable for use for, as per the definition provided above. The action of a medicine may be achieved in, or on the body of a human or animal, by one or more of the following, or any other mechanism: • Pharmacological meaning an interaction typically at a molecular level between a substance or its metabolites and a constituent of the human body which

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: a medicine may be achieved in, or on the body of a human or animal, by one or more of the following, or any other mechanism: • Pharmacological meaning an interaction typically at a molecular level between a substance or its metabolites and a constituent of the human body which results in the initiation, enhancement, reduction, or blockade of physiological functions or pathological processes; • Immunological meaning an action in or on the body that occurs through the stimulation and/or mobilisation of cells and/or products involved in a specific immune reaction; or • Metabolic meaning an action which involves an alteration of the normal chemical processes participating in, and available for, normal body function. Such an action could involve the substance or one or more of its metabolites stopping, starting or changing the rate, extent or nature of a biochemical process, whether physiological or pathological. The fact that a product is itself metabolised does not, however, imply that it achieves its principal intended action by metabolic means. Medical devices A medical device is defined in the Medicines Act as: “Any instrument, apparatus, implement, machine, appliance, implant, reagent for in vitro use, software, material, or other similar or related article, including Group III and IV Hazardous Substances contemplated in the Hazardous Substances Act, 1973 (Act 15 of 1973)— (a) intended by the manufacturer to be used, alone or in combination, for humans or animals, for one or more of the following: (i) diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, treatment, or alleviation of disease; (ii) diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, alleviation of, or compensation for an injury; (iii) investigation, replacement, modification, or support of the anatomy or of a physiological process; (iv) supporting or sustaining life; (v) control of conception; (vi) disinfection of medical devices; or (vii) providing information for medical or diagnostic purposes by means of

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, alleviation of, or compensation for an injury; (iii) investigation, replacement, modification, or support of the anatomy or of a physiological process; (iv) supporting or sustaining life; (v) control of conception; (vi) disinfection of medical devices; or (vii) providing information for medical or diagnostic purposes by means of in vitro examination of specimens derived from the human body; and (b) which does not achieve its primary intended action by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic means, in or on the human or animal body, but which may be assisted in its intended function by such. Where a health product does not achieve its primary intended purpose by pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means, the product is designated as a medical device, e.g. coronary stent. Such a product may, however, be assisted in that effect or purpose by pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means, e.g., a coronary stent coated with a scheduled substance, referred to as a drug eluting stent (DES). A product that is a “related article,” is included in the definition of medical device e.g. operating software in a medical device or a foot switch which is necessary to operate a medical device, is itself classified as a medical device. Combination products In the case of medicines and medical devices, a combination product means a product which may be comprised of two or more components regulated as a medicine and a medical device e.g. a syringe prefilled with a medicine. These components may be physically, chemically, or otherwise combined or mixed and presented as a single entity. A medical device may contain a medicine or a scheduled substance which acts on the body in a manner ancillary to the device. However, where such a substance(s) acts in a manner that is the primary intended mode of action, the product is regulated

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: and presented as a single entity. A medical device may contain a medicine or a scheduled substance which acts on the body in a manner ancillary to the device. However, where such a substance(s) acts in a manner that is the primary intended mode of action, the product is regulated as a medicine rather than a medical device e.g. medicine provided in a metered dose inhaler to treat asthma. Refer to SAHPGL Guideline for Classification of Medical Devices. 4. NON-HEALTH PRODUCTS Cosmetic A cosmetic is defined in the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act, 1972 as: “Any article, preparation or substance (except a medicine as defined in the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 1965 (Act 101 of 1965)) intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on or otherwise applied to the human body, including the epidermis, hair, teeth, mucous membranes of the oral cavity, lips and external genital organs, for purposes of cleansing, perfuming, correcting body odours, conditioning, beautifying, protecting, promoting attractiveness or improving or altering the appearance, and includes any part or ingredient of any such article or substance;” Cosmetics are applied to external parts of the human body with the intended purpose as included in the definition. There is a broad range of products at the cosmetic-medicine-medical device interface. A therapeutic claim may not be made for a cosmetic. In addition, consideration must be given to whether the product is being used, purporting to be suitable for use or manufactured or sold for use for the purposes described in the definition of a medicine or medical device. If such a claim is made and depending on the representation of its intended use and/or composition, the provisions of the Medicines Act may apply. In cases where there is doubt, the appraisal should focus on whether the product is a

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: in the definition of a medicine or medical device. If such a claim is made and depending on the representation of its intended use and/or composition, the provisions of the Medicines Act may apply. In cases where there is doubt, the appraisal should focus on whether the product is a medicine or a medical device. Thus, if the product falls within the definition of a medicine or a medical device and/or a therapeutic claim is made (e.g. reference made ‘to treat or prevent skin disease’), it must be assessed under the medicine or medical device framework. If neither a medicine nor a medical device framework is applicable it could, for example, be classified as a cosmetic. Disinfectant A disinfectant is defined in the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act, 1972 as: “Any article or substance used or applied or intended to be used or applied as a germicide, preservative or antiseptic, or as a deodorant or cleansing material which is not a cosmetic.” A sanitising product may be classified as a medicine, medical device or disinfectant depending on the: (a) intended use and function of the product; (b) composition of the product; (c) surface to which it is applied e.g. the skin of a person or animal or an inanimate surface; and (d) the environment where the product is intended for use. For example, a hand sanitiser for personal hygiene might be considered to be a cosmetic if marketed only for cleansing, but if claims are made that it is antibacterial, it may be classified as a disinfectant or medicine. If, the product’s claims or use align with any human or veterinary therapeutic intent, it is a medicine rather than a disinfectant. Disinfectants used to clean medical instruments and inanimate surfaces in for example, hospitals, operating rooms, intensive care units and

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: it may be classified as a disinfectant or medicine. If, the product’s claims or use align with any human or veterinary therapeutic intent, it is a medicine rather than a disinfectant. Disinfectants used to clean medical instruments and inanimate surfaces in for example, hospitals, operating rooms, intensive care units and burn units will be controlled as medical devices under the Medicines Act. Foodstuff A foodstuff is defined in the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act, 1972 as: “Any article or substance (except a medicine as defined in the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 1965 (Act 101 of 1965)) ordinarily eaten or drunk by a person or purporting to be suitable, or manufactured or sold, for human consumption, and includes any part or ingredient of any such article or substance, or any substance used or intended or destined to be used as a part or ingredient of any such article or substance; In cases where there is doubt, the first consideration must be whether or not the product falls within the definition of a medicine. Products marketed as foods or supplements should not make therapeutic claims as doing so will result in classification as a medicine. Other consumer products In addition, there are other products which do not meet the definition of either a medicine, medical device, foodstuff, cosmetic, or disinfectant and are intended for purposes or uses not covered by these product types. Such products may include, but are not limited to, exercise equipment, software applications and programmes, and information and communication technology. If, however, a product such as a fitness tracker has the functionality of a medical device (e.g. electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring in watches) it should be regulated as a medical device. 5. BORDERLINE PRODUCTS The process for classification of a borderline product should be initiated when there is a

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: communication technology. If, however, a product such as a fitness tracker has the functionality of a medical device (e.g. electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring in watches) it should be regulated as a medical device. 5. BORDERLINE PRODUCTS The process for classification of a borderline product should be initiated when there is a lack of clarity or dispute regarding the correct regulatory pathway to be followed for the classification of the product. In dealing with these situations, the first step is to decide whether or not the product is regulated under the Medicines Act. If it is determined that the product should be regulated by SAHPRA, a recommendation may be made regarding the appropriate regulatory pathway to be applied. Criteria In order to decide the regulatory pathway appropriate for a borderline product, the following factors will be considered: (a) The legal definitions of a medicine, medical device, foodstuff, cosmetic, and disinfectant as provided in the Medicines Act, and the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act, MUST be considered first. In addition, it must be ascertained whether the product itself or a component of the product has been called up for registration in terms of section 14(2) of the Medicines Act. It is also important to check whether the product or a component thereof has been declared as undesirable in terms of section 23 of the Medicines Act in the case of medicines for human use, or section 36A in the case of veterinary medicines. (b) Consideration will also be given to the primary intended purpose and/or use of the product, including any claim(s) made for the product. Both explicit and implicit claims are considered when a product is classified. Explicit claims are stated clearly with no ambiguity regarding their meaning or intent. In contrast, implicit claims use wording which may suggest a therapeutic benefit

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: purpose and/or use of the product, including any claim(s) made for the product. Both explicit and implicit claims are considered when a product is classified. Explicit claims are stated clearly with no ambiguity regarding their meaning or intent. In contrast, implicit claims use wording which may suggest a therapeutic benefit in an indirect manner (for example -Product X is ‘clinically proven’). Even if no therapeutic claim is made (either explicit or implicit), a product may be classified as a medicine or a medical device, if the intrinsic properties of the product are such that there is no other possible use. For example, paracetamol has no other use but as a medicine. When considering the claim made for a product, it is important to note whether more than one property can contribute to the overall effect of the product when used for this indication. To make the necessary distinction, the applicant should, where appropriate do a risk assessment. Specifically, if it is determined that the greater risk is associated with the modification of any somatic, psychic, or organic function, then the safety, quality, and efficacy of the product would be more appropriately assessed under the medicine framework. The reverse will also apply. (c) The method by which the primary mode of action is achieved, e.g., through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means must be considered. The primary mode of action of the product means the most important therapeutic action that makes the greatest contribution to the overall intended therapeutic effect(s) of the product. For example, the primary mode of action of a metered dose inhaler containing a scheduled substance used to treat asthma, is the pharmacological action of the scheduled substance included in the product, and thus it is regulated as a medicine. In another example, however, the primary mode of action

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: product. For example, the primary mode of action of a metered dose inhaler containing a scheduled substance used to treat asthma, is the pharmacological action of the scheduled substance included in the product, and thus it is regulated as a medicine. In another example, however, the primary mode of action of a drugeluting stent, is for the stent to keep the blood vessel open. The scheduled substance coated onto the stent has the secondary role of reducing the risk of blood clotting in the blood vessel. The product is thus regulated as a medical device. (d) The composition of the product the presence of, for example, a scheduled substance, in a product that is making a therapeutic claim, would make the product unsuitable for designation as a cosmetic or foodstuff. (e) The classification of similar products on the market and/or in other regulatory jurisdictions may be considered by SAHPRA but will not be binding. It must be emphasised that classification is done on a case-by-case basis with that applied in other jurisdictions used for guidance only, with final decisions based on South African legislation and context. The criteria above may not be given equal weight in support of a decision, as some factors may be more important to consider in one circumstance versus another. Not all criteria need to be applied if a decision can be reached after the examination of one or a few criteria. If the standard criteria do not lead to a clear decision, supplementary considerations may be considered. The final decision is dependent on the overall consideration. See decision tree in Annexure A Once a product has been classified as a medicine or medical device in terms of the Medicines Act, further classification would be applied in accordance with the Act, regulations, and applicable guidelines as

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: be considered. The final decision is dependent on the overall consideration. See decision tree in Annexure A Once a product has been classified as a medicine or medical device in terms of the Medicines Act, further classification would be applied in accordance with the Act, regulations, and applicable guidelines as determined by SAHPRA. For example, a medicine could be classified into a category as provided in Regulation 9 of the General Regulations published in terms of the Medicines Act. A medical device would be further classified in accordance with SAHPGL-MD-04 Classification of Medical Devices and IVDs. Request for classification of a borderline product The process for classification of a borderline product may be initiated by a prospective applicant before the submission of an application for registration of a health product in terms of the Medicines Act. Alternatively, the process may be proposed to the applicant by SAHPRA after consideration of an application for registration of a product. In either case, the applicable fee is payable by the applicant. Recommendations as to whether a borderline product falls under the jurisdiction of the Medicines Act are made by a Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) appointed by the Chief Executive Officer of SAHPRA. The TAC will consist of representatives of relevant units within SAHPRA and external experts in the areas of foodstuffs, cosmetics, and disinfectants. SAHPRA will provide the decision to the applicant as to whether the product is deemed to be a medicine, medical device or scheduled substance regulated under the Medicines Act. If it is deemed to fall outside the jurisdiction of SAHPRA, a recommendation may be made to the applicant regarding on an appropriate alternative entity e.g. the Food Control Directorate of the National Department of Health for further input. SAHPRA may change its view regarding the classification of the product

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: If it is deemed to fall outside the jurisdiction of SAHPRA, a recommendation may be made to the applicant regarding on an appropriate alternative entity e.g. the Food Control Directorate of the National Department of Health for further input. SAHPRA may change its view regarding the classification of the product in the event of any information or evidence that has a bearing on the status of the product. This may relate to a change in the legislation relating to the product (for example definitions), a change in scientific knowledge or even the way in which the product is packaged, promoted, or presented. SAHPRA can provide no assurance that any product, including products under development, will not subsequently be reclassified (for example, as a medicine or medical device). SAHPRA will engage with the holder of the certificate of registration, or the applicable licence holder regarding such a change in classification. SAHPRA must also be informed if there is an intention to make a change to the claims made relating to a product or to the composition thereof. Regulatory compliance In cases where a product is being marketed which may be considered to be a health product but is not appropriately registered or authorised by SAHPRA, such a health product may also be referred to the TAC, referred to in 5.2 above in cases where there is uncertainty and/or a dispute concerning the classification thereof. 6. SUBMITTING AN APPLICATION An application form must be submitted to SAHPRA. The completed submission must include the following documentation: (a) Table of contents (paginated with hyperlinks to sections); (b) Cover letter; (c) Labelling including the professional information, patient information leaflet, and/or label (where applicable); (d) Information for use, user manual, marketing material, or brochure (where applicable); (e) Safety data sheet (where applicable); (f) Report of the

title: This guideline provides information on the process to be followed when the appropriate regulatory pathway
text: the following documentation: (a) Table of contents (paginated with hyperlinks to sections); (b) Cover letter; (c) Labelling including the professional information, patient information leaflet, and/or label (where applicable); (d) Information for use, user manual, marketing material, or brochure (where applicable); (e) Safety data sheet (where applicable); (f) Report of the results on developmental work (where applicable); (g) Proposed classification with supporting rationale, including composition of the product, primary and secondary (where applicable) mode of action with supporting evidence (where applicable), and any proposed claims (explicit and/or implicit); (h) Risk assessment file (in accordance with ISO 14971 in the case of medical devices and ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management Guidelines in the case of medicines) and, where applicable, a risk management plan; (i) Classification of the product in other jurisdictions recognised by SAHPRA (where relevant); (j) Proof of payment. The applicant must ensure that all relevant fields are completed, and all supporting documentation is attached. Incomplete applications will be identified as deficient, and review will not be progressed until deficiencies are addressed. The prescribed fee and proof of payment must accompany the application. For the current fee payable, refer to the Regulations regarding fees payable in terms of the provisions of the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 1965 (Act 101 Of 1965) as published in the Government Gazette and on the SAHPRA website. The completed application should be submitted electronically to: borderlineproducts@sahpra.org.za using the identified code. Processing of applications Applications for classification of borderline products will be processed by SAHPRA within 30 working days of receiving a complete and valid submission. Upon receiving an application, SAHPRA will screen the application to ascertain whether all required documents as outlined above have been submitted. In cases where outstanding documents or other deficiencies are identified, SAHPRA will inform the applicant within 20 working days.

Upon receiving an application, SAHPRA will screen the application to ascertain whether all required documents as outlined above have been submitted. In cases where outstanding documents or other deficiencies are identified, SAHPRA will inform the applicant within 20 working days. Applicants will be allowed two opportunities to respond to queries. If the applicant fails to submit outstanding documents and/or address deficiencies within a stated timeframe, the application will be considered incomplete and rejected. Any applicable fee already paid will be forfeited. Once all required information has been received and evaluated, SAHPRA will issue a final response letter to the applicant confirming whether the product falls under the jurisdiction of SAHPRA or provide a recommendation as to the entity that could be approached for further advice. This letter will serve as SAHPRA’s official position on the classification of the product. Applicants who are aggrieved by the decision made by SAHPRA may appeal against such a decision in accordance with section 24A of the Medicines Act.2. If it is found that a product does fall under the jurisdiction of SAHPRA, a separate application for registration (for example, for a medicine) must be submitted as a separate process together with the applicable fee. 2 Refer to the SAHPRA guideline SAHPGL-LEG-01 Guideline for appeals against Regulatory Decisions 7. text: GUIDELINE FOR INDUSTRY E-REPORTING This document serves as a guideline to Applicants/ holders of certificates of registration (HCRs) on the method of submission of postmarketing Adverse Event (AE) reports for human medicines through the industry eReporting VigiFlow module. Thus, this guideline must be read in conjunction with the guideline on post-marketing reporting of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) to human medicines in South Africa for guidance on what to report to SAHPRA’s Pharmacovigilance (PV) unit as well as the stipulated timelines. The Authority reserves the right to request any additional information to establish the safety, quality, and efficacy of a medicine and may make amendments to the approved conditions of registration in keeping with the knowledge that is current at the time of consideration of safety data. INTRODUCTION Industry eReporting is a web-based tool that allows Holders of Certificate of Registration (HCRs) or Applicants to submit Individual Case Safety Reports (ICSRs) and Adverse Events Following Immunisation (AEFIs) from an external interface directly to SAHPRA’s National Database in the international standardised format. Industry eReporting further allows for both upload of the international standards for the electronic transmission of ICSR (E2B) XML files, in second revision (R2) or third revision (R3) format, or entering reports via manual data entry by HCRs. Reporting of ICSRs/AEFIs and monitoring thereof, is a viable means of identifying previously unrecognised, rare or serious ICSRs/AEFIs. Every Applicant/ HCR is required to report to the Authority, ICSRs/AEFIs known to them involving their marketed medicines in accordance with the requirements of Regulation 40 of the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 101 of 1965, as amended. The success of the Authority’s ICSRs/AEFIs reporting system depends on the quality, completeness, and accuracy of the information submitted. The Authority makes decisions and takes regulatory actions such as updating a Professional Information and Patient Information Leaflet, restricting the use of a product in certain populations and withdrawal of a product from the South African market, therefore contributing to international data regarding risks and effectiveness of medicines, and imparting health product safety knowledge that benefits all South Africans. 1.1 Purpose This document is intended to guide to HCRs or Applicants on how

title: GUIDELINE FOR INDUSTRY E-REPORTING
text: product in certain populations and withdrawal of a product from the South African market, therefore contributing to international data regarding risks and effectiveness of medicines, and imparting health product safety knowledge that benefits all South Africans. 1.1 Purpose This document is intended to guide to HCRs or Applicants on how to register and report “reportable” postmarketing adverse event reports for human medicines using Industry eReporting VigiFlow module, in accordance with SAHPRA requirements specified in the Guideline on Post-marketing reporting of ADRs to human medicines in South Africa (SAHPGL-CEM-PV-04). In collaboration with Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC), SAHPRA has launched an Industry e-Reporting tool, already piloted by some countries such as Mexico and Pakistan, to name a few. As of 01 September 2026, HCRs/ Applicants are required to submit post-marketing adverse event reports for human medicines through a manual data entry module or E2B upload module using the new tool of industry e-Reporting. The eReporting for Industry, developed and maintained by the UMC, enables HCRs or Applicants to submit reports directly to the National Database, either by manually entering data or uploading E2B XML files: • The manual entry module is an electronic form based on the ICH-E2B (R3) standard, allowing structured and standardized data entry. This replaces previous hard copy CIOMS form (S01) submissions. • HCRs or Applicants who previously submitted XML reports via email can transition to the E2B module, which supports both R2 and R3 formats. This replaces E2B report submissions via email. Key features of eReporting for Industry include: • Compatibility with the ICH-E2B standard • Preference for structured fields over free-text fields • Use of standardized MedDRA and WHODrug terminology • Ability to attach relevant additional information in PDF format • Immediate transmission of reports to SAHPRA • Submission of follow-up reports by uploading and editing the

title: GUIDELINE FOR INDUSTRY E-REPORTING
text: include: • Compatibility with the ICH-E2B standard • Preference for structured fields over free-text fields • Use of standardized MedDRA and WHODrug terminology • Ability to attach relevant additional information in PDF format • Immediate transmission of reports to SAHPRA • Submission of follow-up reports by uploading and editing the original and previous XML files (available only for manual data entry; see Section 8 for instructions) • Capability to download an electronic acknowledgment receipt (acklog) in XML format NOTE: ‒ Using the MedDRA and WHODrug Global dictionaries for medical coding in reporting adverse events makes it much easier to record and analyze patient data in a consistent and accessible way. Therefore, SAHPRA advises HCRs to use both MedDRA and WHODrug while reporting to ensure proper terminologies are used in reporting, as our database terminologies are coded based on these dictionaries. In the future, SAHPRA will make the use of MedDRA and WHO-Drug mandatory for reporting adverse events by all HCRs. 1.2 Scope This guide covers all reportable post-marketing adverse event reports for human medicines received by HCRs or Applicants from various sources, including consumers, healthcare professionals, literature, and other media sources, as per the Guideline on Post-marketing reporting of ADRs to human medicines in South Africa (SAHPGL-CEM-PV-04). Submission of all post-marketing adverse event reports for human medicines includes: • Initial reports • Follow-up reports • Nullification of reports • Duplicate reports handling Reporting of ADRs/ AEFIs and Serious Adverse Events (SAEs) related to unregistered medicines, obtained via section 21 of the Medicines and Related Substances Control Act, active pharmaceutical ingredients used in compounded medicines (Category B), registered and marketed veterinary medicines (Category C), incident reports for medical devices, and in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) through the Industry eReporting VigiFlow Portal is not permitted. 2. LEGAL PROVISION This document is intended for HCRs or Applicants. In accordance with Regulation 40 issued in terms of the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 101 of 1965, as amended. (1) A person who has applied for the registration of a medicine in terms of section 15 of the Act, a holder of a certificate of registration in respect of a medicine or scheduled substance, or a holder of a licence in terms of section 22C (1) (b) must inform the Authority, in the manner and within the timeframe as determined by the Authority. A holder of certificate of registration (HCR)/Applicant and Licence Holder must inform the Authority of any: (a) new or existing quality, safety or effectiveness concerns related to any medicine or scheduled substance, including but not limited to adverse drug reactions; and (b) risk management activities associated with paragraph (1). (2) A person who has applied for registration of a medicine in terms of Section 15 of the Act, a holder of a certificate of registration in respect of a medicine or scheduled substance, or a holder of a licence in terms of section 22C (1) (b) must maintain or have access to records of the reports and case reports referred to in sub regulation (1) above. 3. These codes are only justified when the system requires a value in a mandatory field in order to submit the report to SAHPRA. Mandatory fields necessary for submission are highlighted in red by the system. If a field contains an NF code and the information is unavailable — but the field is not required for submission — you may leave it blank. In such cases, the system will retain the default NF marker automatically. Common NF codes include: • Unknown – The information is not known. • Asked but unknown – The information was requested but not provided. • Not asked – The information was not requested. • Masked/concealed – The information is intentionally hidden. 3.5.2 Icons and their actions This button allows you to add a corresponding section or

No. You need to verify that the file is sent and accepted by: a) Ensuring that the submission status is “Completed” and b) Checking the acklog to verify the reports in the file were accepted. See also question Q10. Q8. Does status “Completed” mean all reports in a file are successfully received by the regulatory authority? No. “Completed” means the file has been successfully sent from the Industry eReporting tool. To make sure all reports are successfully received by the regulatory authority’s database, the acklog needs to be checked (see also Appendix 2 below). Q9. My database does not upload acklogs – how can I read and understand the acklog manually? Acklog codes are described in Appendix 2 to this document. Q10. What does status “pending” mean? “Pending” means the file has not yet been successfully sent from eReporting, for example if the regulatory authority’s database is temporarily down. eReporting will automatically try to re-send the file within 72 hours. Q11. How long will the submission status and acklogs be visible in the ‘Submission status’ tab? Thirty-five (35) days after submission, the information and corresponding acklogs will no longer be available in Industry eReporting. GENERAL FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS Q12. Can I use eReporting for Industry as my own database? No, eReporting for Industry is a one-way submission system and does not function as a database for HCR . Q13. Can I submit PDF or Excel files through eReporting for Industry? No, submissions must be made either through manual data entry or via E2B Upload (XML format). Q14.

No, the system is intended for reporting cases that occur within South Africa. Submission of foreign-sourced ICSRs to SAHPRA is outlined in the guideline: Post-marketing Reporting of Adverse Drug Reactions for Human Medicines in South Africa Q16. What are the minimum criteria for submitting a report? A valid report must include: • An identifiable reporter • An identifiable patient • At least one suspected drug • At least one adverse reaction Q17. Can I save a case and complete it later? No, the system does not support saving drafts. You must complete, submit, or download the report in a single session. Downloading the report is only possible if it meets the minimum submission criteria outlined in the previous question. Note that any unsaved data will be lost upon logout. Q18. Is there a time limit for entering a case? There is no fixed time limit, but inactivity will result in automatic logout for security reasons. Keep interacting with the system to maintain your session. Q19. What if I forgot to download the report after submission? In the Manual Data Entry module, how is the WWUID (Worldwide Unique Case Identification) generated? The WWUID consists of two parts: • Constant section: A 2-letter Country ISO code followed by the HCR Short Name. • Variable section: A unique, consecutive number of at least 5 digits. When entering a report, the constant part is automatically set by the system and should not be modified. You are responsible for assigning the variable part, starting with 00001 for your first report. Each subsequent report must have a unique, incremented number to ensure proper identification. Q21. If your company represents multiple HCRs or CROs, you must notify the SAHPRA of the required identifiers for each entity you represent. These include: • Long name • Short name • Sender ID • Sender organization Recommended configuration: If, for example, PV Company A represents HCR B, you should: • Use HCR B’s identifiers (short name, sender ID, sender organization) • Format the long name as: Long name HCR B (PV Company A) This format ensures that the report is correctly attributed to HCR B while indicating that PV Company A is acting on its behalf. text: GUIDELINE FOR THE COMPLETION OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION OF COMPLIANCE INFORMATION FORM (OF-RDN-NM-06A, REPLACING OLD FORM: 41BM-2) The objective of this guideline is to give clear guidance on the Annual Submission of Compliance Information process from the perspective of an importer/ License Holder and Completion of the Annual submission of Compliance Information Form (OF-RDN-NM-06A, replacing Old Form: 41BM-2). Document History Final Version Reason for Amendment Effective Date − First issue. November 2024 − This guideline replaces the old 41BM-2A, the ASOCI-Guidelines and Corrections that were not aligned to SAHPRA’s QMS documentation structure August 2026 DR BOITUMELO SEMETE-MAKOKOTLELA CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER Glossary Abbreviation/ Term Meaning ASOCI Annual Submission of Compliance Information License Holder Refers to the holder of a licence, granted by the Regulator, under the Hazardous Substances Act (Act no. 15 of 1973). MEDSALE Database used to capture licensing information on an Oracle platform SAHPRA South African Health Products Regulatory Authority 1. INTRODUCTION The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) is mandated, in terms of the Hazardous Substances Act, 1973 (Act No. 15 of 1973) ("the Act") and the Regulations promulgated thereunder, to regulate the importation, sale, letting, use and continued compliance of listed electronic products, including electromedical devices. In fulfilment of this mandate, SAHPRA requires all Licence Holders of licensed electromedical devices to demonstrate continued compliance with the conditions of their licences through the annual submission of current regulatory and conformity assessment information. Licence Condition 9 forms an integral part of every licence issued in respect of an electromedical device and requires Licence Holders to maintain current conformity assessment documentation and to provide such information to SAHPRA upon request or during the annual compliance review process. The Annual Submission of Compliance Information (ASOCI) process enables SAHPRA to verify the continued validity of conformity assessment documentation, regulatory certification and

title: GUIDELINE FOR THE COMPLETION OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION
text: electromedical device and requires Licence Holders to maintain current conformity assessment documentation and to provide such information to SAHPRA upon request or during the annual compliance review process. The Annual Submission of Compliance Information (ASOCI) process enables SAHPRA to verify the continued validity of conformity assessment documentation, regulatory certification and other supporting information to ensure that licensed electromedical devices continue to comply with the applicable legislative and regulatory requirements throughout the validity period of the licence. 1.1 PURPOSE The purpose of this Guideline is to prescribe the regulatory requirements, administrative procedures and compliance obligations applicable to Licence Holders required to complete and submit the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF-RDN-NM-06A), which replaces the legacy Form 41BM-2. This Guideline establishes a uniform administrative framework for the annual submission, assessment and maintenance of compliance information relating to licensed electromedical devices and provides guidance on the regulatory actions that may arise during the annual compliance review process. More specifically, this Guideline sets out the requirements relating to: • the annual distribution of the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form; • the submission of annual compliance information by Licence Holders; • the assessment and verification of submitted information by SAHPRA; • requests for additional information or clarification, where necessary; • the updating of regulatory compliance records; • regulatory action arising from non-submission, late submission, incomplete submission or the submission of deficient information; • the cancellation of licences where regulatory requirements are not satisfied; and • the issuance of updated licence documentation following completion of the annual compliance review process. 1.2 SCOPE This Guideline applies to every Licence Holder holding one or more valid licences issued by SAHPRA in respect of electromedical devices to which Licence Condition 9 applies. The provisions of this Guideline are applicable to: • importers of listed electromedical devices; •

title: GUIDELINE FOR THE COMPLETION OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION
text: of the annual compliance review process. 1.2 SCOPE This Guideline applies to every Licence Holder holding one or more valid licences issued by SAHPRA in respect of electromedical devices to which Licence Condition 9 applies. The provisions of this Guideline are applicable to: • importers of listed electromedical devices; • Licence Holders authorised to import, sell, let, distribute or otherwise place licensed electromedical devices on the South African market; • authorised regulatory representatives acting on behalf of Licence Holders; • persons responsible for maintaining regulatory documentation relating to licensed electromedical devices; and • SAHPRA personnel responsible for the administration, assessment, processing, maintenance and oversight of licensing and compliance records. This Guideline applies irrespective of whether the licensed electromedical device has been certified under the applicable European Medical Device Directives or Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices (MDR), provided that the conformity assessment documentation remains valid and is recognised under the applicable legislative and regulatory framework. 2. LEGISLATIVE FRAMEWORK This Guideline shall be read in conjunction with the following legislation and subordinate legislation: 2.1 The Hazardous Substances Act, 1973 (Act No. 15 of 1973), which provides the legislative authority for the regulation and control of listed electronic products. 2.2 Regulation R.690 of 14 April 1989, promulgated under the Hazardous Substances Act, governing the licensing of persons engaged in the sale, letting and use of listed electronic products. 2.3 Regulation R.1302 of 14 June 1991, prescribing the Schedule of Listed Electronic Products subject to the licensing requirements of the Act. 3. COMPLETION OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION OF COMPLIANCE INFORMATION FORM (OF-RDN-NM-06A) Licence Holders shall complete and submit the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF- RDN-NM-06A) in accordance with the requirements prescribed in this Guideline. The information submitted shall be complete, accurate, current and supported by the applicable conformity assessment documentation and

text: OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION OF COMPLIANCE INFORMATION FORM (OF-RDN-NM-06A) Licence Holders shall complete and submit the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF- RDN-NM-06A) in accordance with the requirements prescribed in this Guideline. The information submitted shall be complete, accurate, current and supported by the applicable conformity assessment documentation and any additional information that may be required by SAHPRA for the purposes of regulatory assessment. The submission of incomplete, inaccurate, misleading or false information, or the failure to submit the required information within the prescribed timeframe, may constitute non-compliance with the conditions of the licence and may result in regulatory action in accordance with the Hazardous Substances Act, 1973 (Act No. 15 of 1973), the applicable Regulations and the conditions of the licence. Licence Holders shall ensure that all information submitted to SAHPRA remains current throughout the assessment process and shall promptly notify SAHPRA of any material changes affecting the information previously submitted. The following instructions shall be followed when completing the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF-RDN-NM-06A). COLUMN INSTRUCTION (i), (ii) Data provided by SAHPRA – DO NOT ALTER. Indicate corrections to any product model name (ONLY for EXISTING licenses on the attached list) on the separate sheet marked “CORRECTIONS”. Copy the license number from the original list and supply all the other data as required. Strike through and/ or mark as “OBSOLETE” any products that are obsolete or which are not being imported anymore for whatever reason – these licenses will then be cancelled. (iii) Classification and Conformity Assessment Requirements Licence Holders shall indicate the classification of each licensed medical device model in accordance with the applicable conformity assessment legislation, namely: • Annex IX of Council Directive 93/42/EEC (Medical Devices Directive); • Council Directive 90/385/EEC (Active Implantable Medical Devices Directive); or • Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical

text: Conformity Assessment Requirements Licence Holders shall indicate the classification of each licensed medical device model in accordance with the applicable conformity assessment legislation, namely: • Annex IX of Council Directive 93/42/EEC (Medical Devices Directive); • Council Directive 90/385/EEC (Active Implantable Medical Devices Directive); or • Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices (MDR), as applicable. For the purposes of the Annual Submission of Compliance Information, SAHPRA will accept the following evidence of conformity assessment, provided that the documentation remains valid and applicable at the time of submission: • valid certificates issued under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR); • valid legacy certificates issued under Council Directives 93/42/EEC or 90/385/EEC that continue to be recognised during the applicable MDR transitional period; • manufacturer declarations or attestations confirming the continued validity of the certification; and • correspondence issued by the Notified Body, where applicable, confirming the regulatory status of the certification. Note: The provision of the requested information is not mandatory where Annex II has been indicated in Column (iv) of the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form or where the medical device is classified as an Active Implantable Medical Device under the applicable regulatory framework. (iv) Conformity Assessment Procedure Licence Holders shall indicate the applicable Annex(es) applied by the Notified Body during the conformity assessment procedure for each licensed medical device, in accordance with the relevant legislative framework. For devices certified under Council Directive 93/42/EEC (Medical Devices Directive) or Council Directive 90/385/EEC (Active Implantable Medical Devices Directive), the applicable Annex(es) shall be those prescribed for the conformity assessment procedures in terms of the respective Directive. For devices certified under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices (MDR), Licence Holders shall indicate the conformity assessment procedure applied in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Regulation. The information provided shall correspond with the conformity assessment documentation

Submission Format The Annual Submission of Compliance Information process shall be conducted as follows: • SAHPRA shall issue the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF-RDN-NM-06A) to the Licence Holder in Microsoft Excel format. • The Licence Holder shall complete the prescribed form in full and submit the completed form to SAHPRA in Portable Document Format (PDF). • The completed form shall be submitted electronically to the designated SAHPRA email address, Radcon.Asoci@sahpra.org.za. • Forms that are incomplete, submitted in an incorrect format, or submitted together with unsolicited supporting documentation may be returned to the Licence Holder for correction prior to assessment. 4. DISTRIBUTION OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION OF COMPLIANCE INFORMATION FORM 4.1 Compliance Groups For the purposes of the annual compliance process, SAHPRA has categorised Licence Holders into eight (8) compliance groups based on alphabetical order, namely: • A–B • C–F • G–H • I–L • M • N–R • S • T–Z 4.2 Distribution of the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form 4.2.1 SAHPRA shall issue the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form (OF-RDN-NM-06A, replacing Old Form: 41BM-2) electronically to the designated contact person of each Licence Holder within the applicable compliance group. 4.2.2 Distribution of the Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form shall commence annually from 1 April and continue in accordance with the established compliance schedule for each respective compliance group. 4.2.3 The electronic notification shall specify the submission requirements, the prescribed submission period and any additional information necessary to facilitate compliance. 4.3 Submission Period Licence Holders shall submit a duly completed Annual Submission of Compliance Information Form, together with any supporting documentation requested by SAHPRA, within thirty (30) calendar days from the date of the electronic notification. 5. ASSESSMENT OF THE ANNUAL SUBMISSION OF COMPLIANCE INFORMATION 5.1 Receipt of Submissions Completed Annual Submission of Compliance Information Forms shall be submitted to the designated SAHPRA electronic mailbox from which the original notification was issued. 5.2 Assessment of Submissions Upon receipt, submissions shall be acknowledged and allocated to the responsible regulatory scientist for assessment. 5.3 Requests for Additional Information Where the submitted information is incomplete or requires clarification, SAHPRA may request additional information or supporting documentation from the Licence Holder.

text: VARIATIONS GUIDELINE FOR HUMAN AND VETERINARY MEDICINES This document provides recommendations for applicants submitting variation applications for human and veterinary medicines. In addition to this guideline, the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) reserves the right to request additional information to establish the safety, quality and efficacy of a medicine based the knowledge available at the time of evaluation. SAHPRA is committed to ensuring that all registered medicines meet the required quality, safety and efficacy. text: Related Substances Act. 1.1 Purpose The purpose of this document is to inform applicants on how to submit applications for variations to the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) for Category A and C medicines as well as what to expect during assessment of variations . 1.2 Scope The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) has compiled a list of requirements for submission of variations to registered products for human and veterinary medicines as well as biologicals. We encourage applicants to read this guideline together with the relevant classification and codes (Section 3.4 below) and SAHPRA guidelines relevant to each Technical Unit as well as the recent relevant guidelines and templates listed in Appendix A. We have outlined requirements in this guideline as well as classification and codes that are aligned to the framework of the International Council for Harmonisation: Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) and the International Cooperation on Harmonisation: Technical Requirements for Registration of Veterinary Medicinal Products (VICH). SAHPRA commits to global best practices regarding the safety, quality and efficacy of health products. 2. LEGAL PROVISION The Medicines and Related Substances Act No. 101 of 1965, as amended, Section 15. (3) (a) (i) - (iii), specifies medicines, medical devices and/or In Vitro Diagnostics (IVDs) that require registration, which should comply with the prescribed requirements and be safe, efficacious and of good quality. General Regulations of the Medicines and Related Substances Act, Regulation 53 (1) and (2) requires that changes to accepted standards or specifications of the registered product should be submitted to SAHPRA for prior approval and the latter should be granted before the changes are implemented. 3. CLASSIFICATION OF VARIATIONS 3.1 Type IA variations (Notifications): Minor changes that have minimal or no impact on quality, safety, or efficacy of the product. SAHPGL-HPA-06_v8 Page 15 of 37 Type IA variations are split into two categories, with differing procedural treatment: a) Type IAAN: Minor variations that do not require any prior approval but must be notified by the HCR within 12 months following implementation (‘Do and Tell’ procedure). b) Type IAIN: Minor variations that must be notified by the HCR at least 47 working days prior to implementation. If 47 working days lapse from the time the notification was submitted, and SAHPRA has not provided feedback to the HCR, the HCR may implement the variation. Upon submission of notification of Type IAIN to SAHPRA, the Authority may review the Type IAIN notification within 47 working days. If SAHPRA has not sent the HCR its opinion on the application within 47 working days, the application will be deemed implementable. Applicants must satisfy themselves that they meet all the prescribed conditions for the change and submit all required documentation with the submission of variations. The variation codes that require approval from more than one (1) Technical Unit cannot be implemented until approval is received from the respective Technical Unit. Note: Failure to meet the specified conditions in the case of notifications of Type IA and minor variations of Type IAin or provide all necessary documentation in the application, may lead to the immediate rejection of the variation, even if the review time has elapsed. If the rejection letter specifies that the implementation of change should be reversed, and the HCR should withdraw the impacted sections of

title: VARIATIONS GUIDELINE FOR HUMAN AND VETERINARY MEDICINES
text: variations of Type IAin or provide all necessary documentation in the application, may lead to the immediate rejection of the variation, even if the review time has elapsed. If the rejection letter specifies that the implementation of change should be reversed, and the HCR should withdraw the impacted sections of the dossier and revert to the previously approved version within 15 days. If any of the conditions are not met or documents are not available, the variation should be classified as a Type IB and submitted as such. 3.2 Type IB variations (minor variations): Type IB variations are changes that may have minor impact on the overall safety, efficacy and quality of the health product or medicine. Applicants must submit all required documents when they submit application for the variation. SAHPRA may review a minor variations of Type IB submission within 87 working days, unless otherwise indicated. If SAHPRA has not sent the HCR its opinion on the application within 87 working days, the application will be deemed implementable (as applicable depending on the variation code). Failure to meet the specified conditions in the case of notifications of minor variations of Type IB or provide all necessary documentation in the application, may lead to the immediate rejection of the variation, even if the review time has elapsed. The timeline for evaluation of Type IB variations is 87 working days. If no response has been received from SAHPRA within this time, changes may be implemented, however SAHPRA may still reject, request reversal of implementation or request further data after the time has elapsed. Please note that SAHPRA timelines are calculated in working days. If the rejection letter specifies that the change should be unimplemented, the HCR should revert the impacted sections of the dossier back to the latest approved version by

If the rejection letter specifies that the change should be unimplemented, the HCR should revert the impacted sections of the dossier back to the latest approved version by means of a closing sequence within 15 days. Applications which cannot be implemented after 87 working days include changes which need approval from more than one (1) Technical Unit, e.g. change in manufacturer of the finished product, change in primary packer or changes in the PI/PIL. SAHPGL-HPA-06_v8 Page 16 of 37 3.3 Type II variations: Type II variations are changes that could have major impact on the overall safety, efficacy and quality of the health products and/or medicines. The submission for review must be approved by SAHPRA before implementations and the documents required for the changes must be submitted together with the submission. SAHPRA has included the Type II variations classification in this guideline (refer to the relevant classification and codes as referenced below) with a view to facilitating timeous review and approval of Type II variations. Upon submission of Type II variations to SAHPRA, the Authority will review the Type II submission within 220 working days for all variations. NOTE: This guideline lists only the minimum technical data requirements for Type II variations. Applicants are advised to include additional data to support the Type II variation if available. GLF-HPA-06J: Veterinary 3.5 Where to submit applications The SAHPRA Engagement Portal is an online platform designed to facilitate interactions between applicants and SAHPRA. The portal enables applicants to submit and track applications, manage their profiles and ensure compliance with regulatory requirements. File Transfer Protocol (FTP) details must be set under the Organisation Details before attempting to create applications that require eCTD uploads to the SAHPRA FTP Server. These changes can involve different types of variations, but they must be linked to the same marketing authorization and can be grouped together under specific conditions. While grouping of different types of variations (Type IA, Type IB and Type II) is acceptable, variations for different Technical Units should not be grouped in a single submission. For information on the acceptable number of variations to be grouped in a single submission refer to SAHPRA engagement portal communications. There should be a clear link or relationship between the grouped variations. For example, a Type II variation for a new indication might be grouped with Type IAin variations for PI/PIL updates affecting the new indication. Type I variations may be submitted with Type II variations; however, the Type I variations are not implementable until the entire variation submission is approved. title: GUIDELINE ON MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTING
text: GUIDELINE ON MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTING GROUP III AND GROUP IV HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES This guideline delineates the mandatory regulatory framework of the Radiation Control Inspectorate sub-unit including the inspection requirements to all Group III and Group IV Hazardous Substances, in terms of the Hazardous Substances Act No. 15 of 1973 and Regulations R1332 and R247. The guideline further provides directions to all holders of Group III and Group IV Hazardous Substances on maintaining compliance with the applicable provisions of the Act and relevant regulations. It sets out the minimum requirements and standard to be adhered to during routine, investigative, and enforcement inspections. R 1302 Regulation related listed electronic products R 690 Regulation related to import of Group III hazardous substances R1332 Regulation concerning the control of electronic products R246 Regulation related to exclusion and exemptions R247 Regulations related to Group IV Hazardous Substances Act RPO Radiation Protection Officer SAHPRA South African Health products Regulatory Authority INTRODUCTION The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) is mandated, in terms of the Hazardous Substances Act No. 15 of 1973 as amended, to regulate, control, and monitor the production, acquisition, importation, exportation, possession, disposal, use, operation, letting, sale, and installation of Group III and Group IV hazardous substances, in order to protect workers, the public, and the environment from radiationrelated harm. Group III and Group IV hazardous substances outline varying levels of radiological risk depending on the nature of the radioactive material, the activity involved, and the way they are used. Effective inspection of facilities and practices involving these substances through a graded regulatory approach is therefore essential to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements and adherence to radiation safety principles. This guideline provides a standardised framework, consistent with SAHPRA's regulatory approach, promoting uniform, transparent, and effective inspections of Group III and Group IV hazardous substances. 1.1 Purpose The purpose of this guideline is to: Define the minimum requirements for conducting inspections of facilities and activities involving Group III and Group IV hazardous substances. Provide guidance to SAHPRA inspectors on the inspection process, focus areas, and compliance expectations. Promote a risk-based and consistent inspection approach aligned with SAHPRA’s Radiation Control framework. The goal is to ensure the licence or authority holders understand the entire process and are fully prepared to meet all requirements. 1.2 Scope This guideline

title: GUIDELINE ON MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTING
text: SAHPRA inspectors on the inspection process, focus areas, and compliance expectations. Promote a risk-based and consistent inspection approach aligned with SAHPRA’s Radiation Control framework. The goal is to ensure the licence or authority holders understand the entire process and are fully prepared to meet all requirements. 1.2 Scope This guideline applies to: All facilities, institutions, and users authorized or required to be authorized to possess, use, store, transport, or dispose of Group III and Group IV hazardous substances. The guideline covers routine, announced, unannounced, follow-up, and compliance inspections but does not replace the requirements set out in legislation, licensing or authorisation conditions, or applicable SAHPRA policies. LEGAL PROVISION This guideline is issued in terms of the following legal instruments: Hazardous Substances Act No. 15 of 1973, as amended, Regulations promulgated under the Hazardous Substances Act relating to Group III and Group IV hazardous substances, Conditions of licencing/ authorization issued by SAHPRA, and Applicable national standards, codes of practice, and international guidance adopted or recognized by SAHPRA. Compliance with this guideline does not exempt any License or Authority Holder from complying with the Act, regulations, or specific licensing or authorization conditions. Where there is a conflict between this guideline and the Act, regulations, licensing or authorization conditions, the latter shall prevail. RADIATION CONTROL INSPECTION PROCESSES Radiation Control inspections shall be conducted by SAHPRA Radiation Inspector appointed in accordance with Hazardous Substance Act, section 8 and shall follow a graded, risk-informed approach. 3.1 Pre-Inspection Activities Review of the licence or written authority, scope, and conditions. Review of previous inspection findings, non-compliances, and corrective actions. Assessment of the radiological risk profile, type of practice, and compliance history. Determination of inspection frequency and inspection scope based on the graded approach. 3.2 On-Site Inspection Opening meeting with management and the Radiation Protection Officer (RPO) or

title: GUIDELINE ON MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTING
text: scope, and conditions. Review of previous inspection findings, non-compliances, and corrective actions. Assessment of the radiological risk profile, type of practice, and compliance history. Determination of inspection frequency and inspection scope based on the graded approach. 3.2 On-Site Inspection Opening meeting with management and the Radiation Protection Officer (RPO) or responsible person. Verification of compliance with legislative and licencing/ authorization requirements. Inspection of facilities, equipment, storage areas, and safety systems. Review of documentation, records, and training evidence. Interviews with relevant staff involved in the use or supervision of hazardous substances. Ensuring controlled entry and display of emergency contact persons and contact details. 3.3 Post-Inspection Activity Closing meeting to communicate preliminary findings. Classification of inspection findings (e.g. critical/ major, intermediate, minor, observations). Issuing of an inspection report specifying corrective actions and timelines. Follow-up inspections or enforcement actions, where warranted. REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTION OF GROUP III HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES Inspections of Group III hazardous substances shall assess compliance with the following minimum requirements: 4.1 Licensing and Governance Availability of Hazardous Substance Act, 15 of 1973, on site. Availability of Regulations R1302 and 1332, on site. Valid SAHPRA license covering the specific substances, activities, and locations. Appointment and competence of a Radiation Protection Officer or Responsible Person. Appointment of Medical Physicist where applicable. Availability of a documented radiation protection programme and operating procedures. Procedures for incident management and reporting to SAHPRA. 4.2 Radiation Protection and Safety Application of the principles of (ALARA), justification, optimisation and dose limitation. Adequate control of occupational and public exposure. Use of personal dosimetry. Workplace monitoring, where applicable. 4.3 Facilities, Storage and Security Appropriate shielding. Adequate access control, and signage. Measures to prevent unauthorised use (in case of mobile units: loss or theft). 4.4 Equipment and Instrumentation Availability of suitable radiation monitoring instruments. Evidence of calibration. Quality Assurance (QA) programme.

Measures to prevent unauthorised use (in case of mobile units: loss or theft). 4.4 Equipment and Instrumentation Availability of suitable radiation monitoring instruments. Evidence of calibration. Procedures for incident management and reporting to SAHPRA. Occupational dose monitoring records. Current proof of professional registration of all practitioners involved. 4.6 Inspection Frequency (Graded Approach – Group III) Inspection frequency shall be determined based on risk, compliance history, and complexity of the practice, and shall typically be: High-risk Group III practices or poor compliance history: at least once every 12 months. Moderate-risk Group III practices with satisfactory compliance: at least once every 24 months. Low-risk Group III practices with demonstrated sustained compliance: at least once every 36 months. REQUIREMENTS FOR INSPECTION OF GROUP IV HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES Inspections of Group IV hazardous substances shall focus on the following minimum requirements: 5.1 Authorization and Governance Renewed and current Authority detailing specific substances, activities, locations and covering prescribed conditions. Confirmation that the activity falls within the applicable authorization or exemption framework. Appointment and competence of a Radiation Protection Officers (RPO and ARPO). Appointment of Medical Physicists where required. Awareness of Hazardous Substances Act No. 15 of 1973 and Regulations related to Group IV Hazardous Substances, R246 and R247. Availability of a documented radiation protection programme and operating procedures. Procedures for incident management and reporting to SAHPRA. Annually updated practice Internal Rules. Evidence of Annual Returns submitted to Radiation Control: radionuclides sub-unit. Register or documentation for disposal of radioactive waste. Radioactive source register. 5.2 Safe Handling and Use Implementation of basic radiation safety practices.

text: This guideline is intended to provide recommendations to applicants wishing to submit new registration applications, as well as variations, for reliance review-based evaluation. It represents the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority’s (SAHPRA’s) current thinking on the safety, efficacy, and quality of medicines. It is not intended as an exclusive approach. SAHPRA reserves the right to request any additional information to establish the safety, efficacy, and quality of a medicine in keeping with the knowledge current at the time of evaluation. Alternative approaches may be used, but these should be scientifically and technically justified. The Authority is committed to ensuring that all registered medicines will be of the required safety, efficacy, and quality. It is important that applicants adhere to the administrative requirements to avoid delays in the processing and evaluation of applications. text: INTRODUCTION The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) has decided to harmonise certain SAHPRA medicine policies and procedures with those of the European Medicines Agency (EMA). By doing so, SAHPRA will reflect global best practice in terms of the safety, quality and efficacy of health product regulation. In line with this, SAHPRA has adopted the reliance review approach as a pathway for the registration of medicines. This approach allows the Authority to leverage evaluation efforts done by a recognised regulatory authority (RRA) with which it aligns, making its evaluation process more efficient and enhance market access. Please note: Unless mentioned otherwise, where EMA guidelines adopted in South Africa include references to European Union (EU) legislation, the requirements contained in the referenced EU legislation are not applicable to the evaluation of medicines by SAHPRA. South African legislation will apply wherever relevant and current. 1.1 Purpose This guideline is intended to provide information and guidance to applicants/ Holders of Certificate of Registration (HCRs) on the prescribed requirements and process to be followed, in cases where a new registration or variation application is submitted to SAHPRA with the applicant/HCR requesting a reliancebased evaluation. 1.2 Scope This guideline applies to new registration applications for human medicines, including biologicals. It is also applicable to veterinary medicines and variation applications. 2. LEGAL PROVISION The Medicines and Related Substances Act (101/1965), as amended, details under Section 2B(2)(a)(2)(b) that: (2)(a) The Authority may liaise with any other regulatory authority or institution and may, without limiting the generality of this power, require the necessary information from, exchange information with, and receive information from any such authority or institution in respect of – (i) matters of common interest; or (ii) a specification investigation; and (2)(b) enter into agreements to co-operate with any regulatory authority to achieve the objects of

text: of this power, require the necessary information from, exchange information with, and receive information from any such authority or institution in respect of – (i) matters of common interest; or (ii) a specification investigation; and (2)(b) enter into agreements to co-operate with any regulatory authority to achieve the objects of this Act. Regulation 16 to this Act, furthermore, states that: (8) In the case where a medicine in respect of which an application for registration is made is or was registered with any regulatory body outside the Republic, the following information in respect of such medicines shall accompany the application: (a) a copy of the certificate of registration; (b) professional information relating to the medicine; (c) conditions of such registration; and (d) any other information as may be required by the Authority. 3. RELIANCE-BASED EVALUATION PATHWAYS The World Health Organization (WHO) defines reliance as the act whereby the regulatory authority in one jurisdiction may consider and give significant weight to – i.e., totally or partially rely upon – evaluations performed by another regulatory authority or trusted institution in reaching its own decision. The relying authority remains responsible and accountable for decisions taken, even when it relies on the decisions and information of others. Wherever possible, SAHPRA will leverage these pathways, relying on the evaluation efforts of Recognised Regulatory Authorities (RRAs) to reduce evaluation times. Reliance-based evaluation pathways of medicine applications for new registrations and variations in South Africa will follow one of three evaluation/ review pathways: a) Abridged review b) Verified review c) Recognition NOTE: Pathways (a), (b), and (c) replace the prior Abbreviated Medicines Review Process (AMRP). The application follows different reliance-based evaluation pathways between Clinical, Quality and Bioequivalence (see Section 4 below and refer also to the Multiple Application Guideline (SAHPGL-HPA-08) on Clones and Replicas). 4. GENERAL DESCRIPTIONS OF THE RELIANCE-BASED EVALUATION PATHWAYS a) Abridged review: A streamlined review based primarily on full assessment reports from RRAs, replacing the need to evaluate all data (and summaries thereof) submitted in support of an application. b) Verified review: A streamlined review based primarily on verifying, instead of evaluating, information submitted in the application against information that has already been approved by SAHPRA or an RRA. Note that full assessment reports are required for Quality and Bioequivalence PEM-verified reviews as a fallback option for evaluators. c) Recognition: A streamlined registration/ approval process based on directly recognising the outcome of a review from an RRA with which SAHPRA shares a recognition agreement. NOTE: SAHPRA is currently in the process of negotiating recognition agreements with RRAs. Once such an agreement is in place, SAHPRA will publish a framework for the practical implementation thereof. The guiding principle is that applications approved by RRAs with which SAHPRA shares a recognition agreement may not need to be evaluated separately by SAHPRA. Please note that this is not to be confused with collaborative/ work-sharing procedures (e.g., ZAZIBONA). 4.1 SAHPRA’s Recognised Regulatory Authorities To qualify for a reliance evaluation pathway, an application must have been approved by one or more of the RRAs with which SAHPRA aligns itself. For example, a typical application for a generic/ multisource medicine requires a relatively straightforward verification of PIs for Clinical review, however Quality and Bioequivalence face the added complexity of bioequivalence assessments. Consequently, SAHPRA’s reliance pathways are applied independently for Clinical, Quality and Bioequivalence. These documents are available on the SAHPRA website. By choosing the intended pathways enables SAHPRA to conduct technical screening more efficiently and prevents unnecessary delays. Decisions related to an application’s final evaluation pathway and the extent of reliance on an RRA’s evaluation are fully at SAHPRA’s discretion. These decisions will depend on the availability and quality of reliance documentation submitted. SAHPRA will share screening queries to the respective applicant(s) who submitted insufficient reliance documentation, to maximise the number of applications that can qualify for abridged and verified reviews.
