text: Safe Transport of Radioactive Material (No. SSR-6 Rev. 1) See Figure 1 below for a graphic representation of the security levels. FIGURE 1 TRANSPORT SECURITY LEVELS (NSS 9-G) 5. Requirements for Security in the Transport of Radioactive Material 5.1 Prudent Management Practices Prudent Management Practices should be applied to all shipments of radioactive material regardless of material category. These practices are the same basic security precautions that might be applied to any cargo of high value. 1) General security provisions a) The Authority Holder shall ensure that all persons engaged in the transport of radioactive material apply security measures commensurate with their responsibilities and the level of threat. b) Radioactive material shall be transferred only to authorised Authority Holders. c) When radioactive material is temporarily stored at transit sites or makes an expected or unexpected stop, appropriate security measures shall be applied consistent with the measures applied during use and storage. d) The Authority Holder shall have procedures in place to ensure that, if any package is not delivered to the intended recipient at the expected time, an inquiry is initiated about the status of that package. If the package has been lost or stolen or appears to have been tampered with, procedures shall immediately be initiated to locate and recover the package. e) Enclosed lockable vehicles should be used for transportation of radioactive materials. f) Radioactive material must be transported in approved packaging and the transport package must be locked and secured to the vehicle to prevent inadvertent movement during transport. g) Transport containers must be locked inside the vehicle and must be positioned at the maximum distance possible from the passenger compartment. h) If an open vehicle is used, the transport container must be permanently fixed to the vehicle unless it weighs more than 2000 kg. i) Utilising

title: M a r c h
text: during transport. g) Transport containers must be locked inside the vehicle and must be positioned at the maximum distance possible from the passenger compartment. h) If an open vehicle is used, the transport container must be permanently fixed to the vehicle unless it weighs more than 2000 kg. i) Utilising carriers with package tracking systems (e.g., bar code system to monitor the status of the shipment), as appropriate; j) Not leaving packages or conveyances unattended for any longer than is absolutely necessary; k) Providing drivers of road conveyances with effective communication capability; l) Satellite tracking system on vehicle. 5.2 Basic Transport Security Level Requirements (Categories 1, 2, and 3) In addition to Prudent Management Practices, the Basic Transport Security Level Requirements shall be applied to radioactive material that has been evaluated as Category 1, 2, or 3. 5.2.1 Contingency Planning Contingency plans include predefined sets of actions for response to off-normal situations, such as unauthorised acts indicative of attempted unauthorised removal or sabotage, including threats thereof designed to effectively counter such acts. Contingency plans must be developed for all shipments of Category 1, 2, and 3 radioactive materials. The graded approach will be applied such that the level of rigor and detail will be greater for higher category material, with Category 1 being the highest category and requiring the most detail. Category 3 Contingency Plans should include emergency contact telephone numbers and basic driver actions to take if an off-normal event occurs. Category 2 Contingency Plans should include emergency contact telephone numbers of detailed instructions on actions to take if an off-normal event occurs. Category 1 Contingency Plans should include comprehensive instructions for response to off-normal situations based on an analysis of all credible hazards and threats which may arise during the shipment. General notes on developing contingency plans: 

title: M a r c h
text: telephone numbers of detailed instructions on actions to take if an off-normal event occurs. Category 1 Contingency Plans should include comprehensive instructions for response to off-normal situations based on an analysis of all credible hazards and threats which may arise during the shipment. General notes on developing contingency plans:  All safety incidents have a security component if the shipment is halted.  Contingency plans are a working document containing formats, such as flow-charts and bulleted lists.  The credible hazards and threats may be identified using a standardised checklist.  Identify categories of risks using the checklist, for example: o Environmental/Natural o Traffic/Routing o Medical o Mechanical o Malicious act  Each risk category should have a response framework developed so that an individual contingency plan does not need to be developed for every conceivable scenario – the basic actions are the same within each category. If there is a major difference in protocol, then a new plan can be developed (i.e., if there is severe weather inbound, vs a mudslide that damages the road – the severe weather might cause a delay in the shipment, while the mudslide might reroute the shipment, but both natural disasters).  Contingency plans must always support and not hinder first responders, and should never dictate first responder actions (i.e., do not tell the police what to do, and need to be compatible with the police response so that they do not slow down or reduce the effectiveness of the police response).  It is acceptable for security and safety contingency plans to be combined in a single document so that the driver has access to all contingency plans in a single location. 5.2.2 Trustworthiness Determination The Authority Holder shall subject persons engaged in the transport of radioactive material to a trustworthiness determination

title: M a r c h
text: It is acceptable for security and safety contingency plans to be combined in a single document so that the driver has access to all contingency plans in a single location. 5.2.2 Trustworthiness Determination The Authority Holder shall subject persons engaged in the transport of radioactive material to a trustworthiness determination commensurate with their responsibilities. Methods of determining trustworthiness: 1) Criminal history check conducted by the South African Police Service (SAPS). 2) Conflict of interest statement, examples might include self-reported disclosures of any outside business dealings, which could cause a violation of this security guidance or incentives to compromise the security of radioactive material in transport. This statement should be reviewed and approved by a senior management official of the Authority Holder. 3) Drug and Alcohol testing should be administered at randomised intervals and should ensure that personnel performing their duties in the transport of radioactive material are not performing their duties while impaired. 5.2.3 Shipper and Carrier Credentials Each crew member of any conveyance transporting radioactive material shall carry means of identification, such as an official identification document, including an identity document, driver’s license, or passport. This photo identification must be accompanied by a written authorisation from the crew member’s employer, with the names of individuals specifically authorized to perform a given transport. 5.2.4 Written Procedures The Authority Holder shall develop implementation procedures and provide them to crew members. These procedures shall address the application of security measures which have been required as a condition of the Transport Authority issued by the regulatory body. Response procedures should include basic steps on how to respond to an off-normal incident during transport, such as safe parking instructions and emergency points of contact. At a minimum, these procedures should include 24-hour contact information for the Authority Holder’s radiation protection officer, the regulatory body,

title: M a r c h
text: by the regulatory body. Response procedures should include basic steps on how to respond to an off-normal incident during transport, such as safe parking instructions and emergency points of contact. At a minimum, these procedures should include 24-hour contact information for the Authority Holder’s radiation protection officer, the regulatory body, and SAPS. Additionally, they may include emergency contact information for the national emergency centre and emergency services. Emergency services telephone numbers must be obtained from the local service providers. 5.2.5 Security Training The Authority Holder shall ensure that all persons engaged in the transport of radioactive material receive training, including training in the elements of security awareness. Such training shall be provided or verified upon employment and periodically supplemented by retraining. Records of all security training undertaken shall be kept by the Authority Holder and shall be made available, upon request, to the employee and to the Regulatory Authority. Security Awareness training should include the following elements: a) Describe the need for transport security; b) The nature of security-related threats; c) Methods to address security concerns; d) Actions to be undertaken if a security event occurs; and e) Training on the Transport Security Plan, where applicable, and the individual’s role(s) in implementing the Transport Security Plan. 5.2.6 Exchange of security-related information Authority Holders shall cooperate and with the appropriate authorities to exchange information on applying security measures and responding to security incidents. The purpose of information sharing is to ensure uniformity of security throughout the transport; however, information sharing should only be conducted in a manner that is consistent with information protection requirements. 5.2.7 Communications During transport, the Authority Holder should provide the capability for vehicle crew members to communicate with their company or law enforcement to request assistance. This can be executed, for example, by using mobile telephones. Communication

This can be executed, for example, by using mobile telephones. Communication should remain effective throughout the entire journey. Where this is not possible, predefined communication points in the journey should be agreed to in order to provide evidence that the journey is proceeding as planned without incident. 5.2.8 Security Verification Conveyors shall perform security verification inspections of conveyances and shall ensure that these security measures remain effective during transport. This inspection should be documented using a signed and dated checklist prior to shipment departure. Self-Inspections should be conducted to verify that security measures specified in the Prudent Management Practices and Basic Transport Security Level have been implemented as a condition for receiving a Transport Authority. 5.2.9 Receipt Verification The Consignee should have procedures in place to verify that package contents match the expected radioactive material inventory and/or any relevant shipment documents available. The procedures should include provisions for notifying SAHPRA, Consignor, and Conveyor if radioactive material is discovered to be missing. 5.3 Enhanced Transport Security Level Requirements (Category 1 and 2) In addition to Prudent Management Practices and Basic Transport Security Level Requirements, Enhanced Transport Security Level Requirements shall be applied to radioactive material which has been evaluated as Category 1 or 2. 5.3.1 Information Protection Measures should be taken to protect sensitive information relating to transport operations, including detailed information on the schedule and route. Such information should be shared on a need-to-know basis, and includes the security system design and operation, response capability, detection, assessment, and delay capabilities. In addition, computer security is critical to protecting sensitive information. Computers

title: M a r c h
text: protect sensitive information relating to transport operations, including detailed information on the schedule and route. Such information should be shared on a need-to-know basis, and includes the security system design and operation, response capability, detection, assessment, and delay capabilities. In addition, computer security is critical to protecting sensitive information. Computers should be accesscontrolled commensurate to the level of information stored. These systems should be accessible only by persons on a need-to-know basis who have undergone a trustworthiness verification. The primary application for information protection is found in the security plan, which contains the above-mentioned details. 5.3.2 Transport Security Plan A Transport Security Plan is required to be submitted to SAHPRA for all Category 1 and 2 transport applications. The Transport Security Plan for category 2 sources must be reviewed annually. If any aspect of the transport is subcontracted, the Authority Holder shall ensure that the subcontractor complies with the Transport Security Plan. The Transport Security Plan shall include at least the following elements and shall be modified as needed to reflect changes in the threat level: a) Specific allocation of responsibilities for security to competent and qualified persons with appropriate authority to carry out their responsibilities; b) Provision for keeping records of radioactive material packages or types of radioactive material transported; c) Review of current operations and assessment of vulnerability, including intermodal transfer, storage in transit, handling, and distribution as appropriate; d) Clear statements of transport security measures, including training and policies, response to conditions of a higher-level threat, verification of new employees and employment, operating practices, equipment, and other resources; e) Effective procedures and equipment for timely reporting and responding to security-related threats, in addition to breaches of security or security-related incidents; f) Procedures for evaluating and testing Security Plans and procedures for periodic review and update of the

title: M a r c h
text: of new employees and employment, operating practices, equipment, and other resources; e) Effective procedures and equipment for timely reporting and responding to security-related threats, in addition to breaches of security or security-related incidents; f) Procedures for evaluating and testing Security Plans and procedures for periodic review and update of the plans; g) Measures to ensure the security of sensitive transport information contained in the Security Plan; h) Measures to ensure that the distribution of sensitive transport information is limited on a need-to-know basis; i) Measures to monitor the location of the shipment; and j) Where appropriate, details concerning agreements on the point of transfer of responsibility for security. For detailed instructions and an example plan and template, see Annex II of this document (NSS 9-G example TSP). Transport Security Plans must be submitted at the time of the application for authority to transport. SAHPRA will inform the applicant on the details of how a secure submission of the application must be made. 5.3.3 Planning and Coordination The shipper shall provide advance notification to the receiver and SAHPRA of each planned shipment. This advance notification must include details of the mode of transport and the expected shipment schedule. The Consignee shall confirm capability and readiness to accept delivery at the expected time and shall notify the shipper and SAHPRA on receipt or non-receipt within the expected delivery time frame. In the case of routine industrial radiography camera use, or other routine Category 2 users, the details of the transport must be recorded in the source log and be made available to SAHPRA for inspection. No additional notifications are required. This does not apply in cases where a radiography camera is being shipped for the purpose of replacing the source and a notification is required. 5.3.4 Physical Security The physical security system

text: recorded in the source log and be made available to SAHPRA for inspection. No additional notifications are required. This does not apply in cases where a radiography camera is being shipped for the purpose of replacing the source and a notification is required. 5.3.4 Physical Security The physical security system includes those measures that provide detection, delay, and response. 5.3.4.1 Detection At a minimum, detection is provided by the vehicle crew who have been briefed on the Transport Security Plan and have been provided with emergency contact information. The vehicle crew should be instructed to immediately contact law enforcement as well as their RPO if any suspicious activity is observed. NSS 9-G Section 5.48. Electronic intrusion detection and alarms, including duress alarms, should be considered. Electronic intrusion detection technologies can be suitable for providing an immediate indication of an intrusion into the cargo area. Examples of this technology include the following: (a) Balanced magnetic door switches; (b) Light sensors (for closed conveyances); (c) Fibre optic and other electronic seals; (d) Passive infrared, microwave or video motion detection. If electronic intrusion detection systems are implemented, they must be remotely monitored by personnel with training on the correct procedures to follow if an alarm is detected. Enhanced detection will be provided by armed escorts and the RPO accompanying the shipment. Each must be able to communicate with SAHPRA, SAPS, and the Emergency Centre. 5.3.4.2 Delay Locks and seals should be applied to conveyances, compartments or freight containers. Locks and seals should be checked to confirm the integrity before dispatch, after any stops made during the journey and during any intermodal transfer of each radioactive material consignment. If enclosed freight containers are used, verification of the integrity of a door seal is sufficient, and individual seals on packages inside the freight container do

text: checked to confirm the integrity before dispatch, after any stops made during the journey and during any intermodal transfer of each radioactive material consignment. If enclosed freight containers are used, verification of the integrity of a door seal is sufficient, and individual seals on packages inside the freight container do not need to be verified. Lock fittings and components, such as attachment points and tie-downs, should be complementary to the quality and strength of the locks. In cases where chains are unavailable, the package should be contained within an ISO Intermodal Container to provide an additional barrier against direct access to the package. Procedures should be established to ensure the security of keys to conveyances and locks. 5.3.4.3 Response Response is provided by SAPS per their operating procedures. The Authority Holder must include contact information for SAPS in the instructions provided to the crew of the vehicle. 5.3.5 Communications Routine communications may be conducted by mobile telephone. Techniques such as code words and phrases should be used to reduce the amount of sensitive information that is shared over open communications. This does not apply in an emergency. 5.3.6 Pre-shipment Security Verification The Consignor and Conveyor should conduct a pre-shipment security verification of the conveyance and security systems before commencing transport. The purpose of this verification is to ensure that the security measures are implemented as described in the Transport Security Plan and are functioning normally. This verification should ensure that security measures specified in the Prudent Management Practices, Basic Transport Security Level, and Enhanced Transport Security Level have been implemented as a condition for receiving a Transport Authority. NSS 9-G Section 5.52. Corrective actions should be taken upon identifying that one or more elements are deficient. Without corrective actions, shipments should not be undertaken. 5.4 Other Security Measures for Category

All packages shall be tracked during transport to ensure that the status of the package can be determined at any time. Road vehicles transporting Category 1 quantities of radioactive material shall be equipped with automatic and real-time tracking capability. 5.4.3 Additional Physical Security Enhanced detection will be provided by armed escorts, the driver, and the radiation protection officer accompanying the shipment. Enhanced delay will be provided by chain tie-downs/any other tie-down that does not compromise the integrity of the transport container. Inspection and Enforcement 6.1 Regulatory inspection of Vehicles and Information The Authority Holder shall provide inspectors and other officers appointed by the Regulator with immediate access to transport vehicles and locations in which radioactive materials are present to obtain information concerning the status of security and verify compliance with the Authority conditions. Each Authority Holder shall make available to the Regulator information and records regarding security as requested. 6.2 Enforcement An Authority Holder who violates any security-related condition of an authority, is subject to the following enforcement actions by the Regulator. (1) An Inspection Report requiring corrective action within a specified time; (2) A Notice of Violation issued by the Regulator stating the alleged violation and requiring the holder of an authority, within 20 business days of the date of the notice or other specified time, to submit a written reply, including: (a) Corrective steps, if any, which have been taken, and the results achieved; (b) Further corrective steps which will be taken; and (c) The date when full compliance will be achieved. (3) An Order issued by the Regulator modifying, suspending, or revoking an authority, seizing radioactive material or placing an embargo on its use, or taking such other action as may be proper. The order: (a) alleges the transgressions of the act in terms whereof the authority holder may be criminally charged; (b) provides that the holder of an authority must file a written answer to the order within 20 business days of its date, or such other time as may be specified in the order; (c) provides for consideration by the Regulator the answer and modification or withdrawal of

Organisational structure This subsection specifies the organisational structure of the entities involved in the transport, describing the chain of command, including the names of responsible personnel. 6.2. Allocation and transfer of responsibilities This subsection describes the responsibilities of all organisations and persons engaged in the transport of radioactive material, including how and when security responsibilities are transferred. 7. I N F O R M A T I O N MANAGEMENT This section specifies how all information will be managed, particularly for security-sensitive information. Reference to other information management procedures can be used. 7.1. Information security This subsection describes how the security of information will be ensured. Reference to other information management procedures can be used. 7.1. Information security This subsection describes how the security of information will be ensured. This description might include identification of sensitive information, classification review and marking, reproduction restrictions, distribution (i.e., authorised access and need-to-know), storage requirements and destruction. 7.2. Records retention This subsection identifies who has responsibility for retaining records to ensure records are handled in accordance with regulatory requirements and procedures (can include requirements for shippers, carriers and receivers). 8. Routing This subsection specifies routes and associated in-transit storage and intermodal transfer locations. The information provided here includes the following:  Planned (primary) and alternate routes for all modes of transport, including criteria for when the alternate routes will be used;  Process for pre-shipment evaluation of routes, assessment of vulnerabilities;  Identification of any in-transit storage and intermodal transfers, including security arrangements. 8.2. Transport security system This subsection describes the security system, including specific security measures (based on the transport security level of the shipment) and other arrangements that will be used. 8.2.1. Conveyance This subsection describes the conveyances (road, rail, air, water), including any special requirements for the conveyances. 8.2.2. Operations command and control This subsection identifies command and control procedures for normal and emergency operations. This information includes achain of command structure, decision-making authority, points of contact and identification of response agencies. This information includes achain of command structure, decision-making authority, points of contact and identification of response agencies. Nuclear security measures This subsection identifies the nuclear security measures to be used during transport. These measures include those used to provide detection, delay and response. Examples of these measures include the following:  Tamper-indicating devices and seals (packages and conveyances);  Locks (single or multiple) for packages, cargo compartment, and conveyance (e.g., door keys, ignition keys);  Secure tie-downs and over-packs;  Immobilising devices. This subsection also identifies the process for authorising alternative measures (i.e., when a feature is not operational or available). 8.2.3. It also describes any system for tracking the conveyances, including identification of the location at which shipment monitoring will occur. 8.2.4. Maintenance and testing of systems and equipment This subsection addresses how all of the systems involved in the shipment(s) (such as communications and tracking) are maintained and tested. This subsection also addresses the checking and testing of all mission-related equipment that will be performed before the beginning of the transport. It also specifies periodic testing requirements. This section identifies the range of incidents that might need response measures to be initiated, describes the appropriate response measures, and clearly defines the response resources. 1.1. Emergency and contingency response This subsection identifies handling responses of non-nuclear or non-radiological emergency and security-related incidents; it is not to be confused with specific arrangements for response to a nuclear or radiological emergency. Response actions to be included in this subsection are actions that will be taken by crew members, the transport control centre or other operations centres; shipper and receiver technical support staff; emergency response units along the route; escort personnel (if present); guard or security force (if present), and response forces. Emergency situations can include road closure, vehicle breakdown, vehicle accidents, and driver illness. Corresponding emergency arrangements could include the availability of backup vehicles and drivers, capabilities for towing and lifting, and plans for use of safe havens. This information could include the types of communications equipment used and features to ensure the security of communications. 1.3. Reporting of threats and incidents This subsection describes reporting requirements, including types of events that must be reported, to whom and how the event will be reported, and the timeframe for reporting.

text: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND LACTATION This document has been prepared to serve as a guideline for the preparation of applications to conduct clinical trials in South Africa. It represents the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority’s [SAHPRA] current thinking on pregnancy and lactation for clinical research in South Africa. It is not intended as an exclusive approach, and SAHPRA reserves the right to request any additional information and may make amendments in keeping with the knowledge that is current at the time. Document History Final Version Reason for Amendment Effective Date First issue – published for implementation 01 June 2026 DR BOITUMELO SEMETE-MAKOKOTLELA CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER Glossary Abbreviation/ Term Meaning ABPI The Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry CIOMS Council for international organizations of medical sciences COVID The disease Covid-19 CTC Clinical Trial Committee CTF1 Clinical trials application form DSMB Data and Safety Monitoring Board HIV Human immunodeficiency virus IP/IMP Investigational product/ Investigational Medicinal Product IVDs In vitro diagnostic medical devices LMIC Lowand Middle-Income Countries NCE New chemical entity UN United Nations PK and PD Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics SAD & MAD Single Ascending Dose and Multiple Ascending Dose SAGCP The South African Good Clinical Practice guidelines SAE/AESI/AEs Serious adverse event/ adverse event of special interest/ adverse events SAHPRA The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority SOP Standard Operating Procedure TIE Time, Inconvenience and Expenses INTRODUCTION All clinical trials related to pregnancy and lactation need to be rigorously scientifically, ethically, statistically, and clinically sound and appropriate to both the needs of this group of participants and important to the needs of the South African and the rest of the world thereby ensuring maximal safety and minimal risk as well as critical benefits to Women of childbearing age, foetuses and neonates/ infants. These studies therefore need to be in

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: the needs of this group of participants and important to the needs of the South African and the rest of the world thereby ensuring maximal safety and minimal risk as well as critical benefits to Women of childbearing age, foetuses and neonates/ infants. These studies therefore need to be in conformance with the latest and current guidelines regarding Good Clinical Practice SAGCP, National Department of Health Guidelines for Ethics and Research as well as the latest Declaration of Helsinki, ICH-GCP and CIOMS as well as other relevant clinical research guidelines. Clinical research with individuals, groups, or communities in situations of vulnerability is only justified if it is responsive to both their health needs and priorities as well as those of groups and communities who stand to benefit from the resulting knowledge, practices, or interventions. Such studies further need to conform to the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, and relevant laws and regulations in the Republic. While pregnancy is not considered a disease or illness, it needs to be recognized that there are physiological and psychological changes in pregnancy, foetal and neonatal/ infant milieus, which may exhibit unique PK and PD parameters. There may be unique pathological conditions contributing to the need to study interventions in these participants. Purpose There is a need to be more inclusive, and retention of, with pregnancy and lactation related interventional trials involving investigational products (new and existing chemical entities) and medical devices and IVDs whilst not compromising safety, participant benefit, and protection of the participant, in all studies, Phases 1 to 4. Studies in this domain can be planned either as independent study or a sub study or as continued pregnancy follow up embedded within studies or sub studies with other objectives. Scope This guideline applies

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: compromising safety, participant benefit, and protection of the participant, in all studies, Phases 1 to 4. Studies in this domain can be planned either as independent study or a sub study or as continued pregnancy follow up embedded within studies or sub studies with other objectives. Scope This guideline applies to all clinical trials (Phase 1-4). It establishes a framework for: Protection of participants in clinical trials related to pregnancy and lactation (maternal, foetal and neonatal/ infant). Enabling appropriate conduct and successful outcome of clinical trials in pregnancy and lactation. To guide stakeholders on clinical trials during pregnancy and lactation. To guide management of participants' outcomes for participants who become pregnant and/or lactate during clinical trials not primarily designed for reproductive health. In case of studies involving medical devices/ IVDs (e.g., diagnostic assays and kits, monitoring systems), refer also to the Guidelines on clinical investigation requirements on https://www.sahpra.org.za/medical-devicesand-in-vitro-diagnostics-guidelines. LEGAL PROVISION These guidelines are established in terms of Regulations issued in sections 90(s) and 72(6)(c) of the National Health Act, Act No. 61 of 2003, as well as Regulation 30 of the Medicines and Related Substances Act, Act No. 101 of 1965. All role players involved in clinical trials related to pregnancy and lactation should also be familiar with the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, national and international guidelines, including but not limited to the following current versions or their successors: SA GCP South African Ethics in Health Research Guidelines: Principles, Processes and Structures Universal Declaration of Bioethics and Human Rights Applicable legislation and associated regulations ICH GCP Declaration of Helsinki ABPI (Section Special Populations: Women) PREGNANCY Pre-submission Meetings Stakeholders should, at both regulatory request and/ or self-decision, engage with SAHPRA to ensure aspects of the planned study are discussed for smooth progress and regulatory success (refer to communications

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: Human Rights Applicable legislation and associated regulations ICH GCP Declaration of Helsinki ABPI (Section Special Populations: Women) PREGNANCY Pre-submission Meetings Stakeholders should, at both regulatory request and/ or self-decision, engage with SAHPRA to ensure aspects of the planned study are discussed for smooth progress and regulatory success (refer to communications with SAHPRA guidelines). Pregnant or breastfeeding women should be included in human clinical trials where possible, i.e., when safety and other relevant information are available during a clinical trial. This is to ensure that appropriate knowledge about NCEs for this group of people is developed. Public Health Emergencies The recent COVID and HIV pandemics have illustrated the need for adequate study and planning of the use of IPs in pregnancy and lactation. Studies that address the scenarios of public health emergencies will be prioritized at the CTC level to expedite early implementation. More frequent vigilance in terms of early SAE/ AESI reporting or progress reports or applicant engagement, or interim analyses by DSMBs or sponsors may be required at regulatory discretion. Prevailing Evidence (Non-clinical/ Clinical) In preparation for human studies, non-clinical developmental and reproductive safety and toxicology studies must be done along with genotoxic studies. These studies must be available for any SAHPRA submission for evaluation. All clinical studies in pregnant women require clinical data in non-pregnant participants before extending to pregnant participants. Outcomes of these studies will guide extension to pregnancy and lactation. As there are maternal and fetal differences in each trimester, any study needs to take cognisance of the appropriateness of the study design per trimester. Clinical studies incorporating pregnancies In specific, predetermined, pre-discussed situations, clinical studies may progress directly to pregnant and lactating participants. If the applicant/ sponsor determines that proceeding with trials in pregnancy is appropriate, then the following approaches/ actions (in no specific order)

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: of the appropriateness of the study design per trimester. Clinical studies incorporating pregnancies In specific, predetermined, pre-discussed situations, clinical studies may progress directly to pregnant and lactating participants. If the applicant/ sponsor determines that proceeding with trials in pregnancy is appropriate, then the following approaches/ actions (in no specific order) need to be considered and/ or incorporated into the development strategy: Recruitment of pregnant individuals in each trimester into ongoing and/ or subsequent clinical trials, Removal of mandatory contraception requirements in ongoing and/or subsequent clinical trials, Implementation of study(ies) specifically designed to be conducted in pregnant individuals if needed, Ongoing participation of individuals who become pregnant during clinical trials (source: ICH E21 Guidelines), and Management of pregnancies where contraceptive methods have failed requires a safety review before concluding on the risk-benefit of the IP. Pregnant individuals must continue in the study but not receive any further IP (unless otherwise specified in the protocol or if there is a demonstrated positive risk-benefit). The baby should be followed up for an appropriate period, preferably up to a minimum of 18 months. 3.4.1 Scenario of Failed Contraception in Studies where WOCBP are enrolled with mandatory contraception Women of childbearing potential may experience a “breakthrough pregnancy” despite the implementation of a trial-required method of contraception. Several outcomes may be presented depending on an informed choice and intensive information sharing by the investigator and/ or sponsor, such as: Continuation of pregnancy with or without IP under strict(er) investigator/ sponsor guidance and surveillance until birth and close evaluation of infants thereafter, Termination of Pregnancy and no continuation in the study, Possible unblinding, Reporting to the regulatory authority, Re-evaluation of participant insurance if needed, and Pregnant participants should be retained in studies as far as possible, and allowance should be made to incorporate obstetric and post-natal and

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: close evaluation of infants thereafter, Termination of Pregnancy and no continuation in the study, Possible unblinding, Reporting to the regulatory authority, Re-evaluation of participant insurance if needed, and Pregnant participants should be retained in studies as far as possible, and allowance should be made to incorporate obstetric and post-natal and paediatric care within the study. Phase 1 Studies - (Refer to first-in-human, Phase I guideline) 3.5.1 In exploratory Phase 1 studies, (SAD and MAD) women should typically be of “non-childbearing potential”. (ABPI). 3.5.2 Generally, Phase I trials should not be done in pregnant women. 3.5.3 Should the trials be required in pregnant women, they must be performed at a later stage of clinical IP(s) development once there is data from non-pregnant participants. Procedures Procedures should be carried out at minimal risk and at the very least within the standards of antenatal care. The following items should be summarized and further described and included in the site capacity as per Section 2.4 of the new trial application (CTF1). The SOP should further be provided for the items below: An antenatal and postnatal care plan must be provided, Heath care professionals experienced in ultrasound should be available, Midwives and obstetricians as well as other Health care professionals with adequate experience should be available for delivery, Site should include investigators with experience in neonatal management, Participants should have easy access to antenatal and labour care, Procedural obstetrics (Chorionic villous sampling, amniocentesis) should be done if clinically indicated, Cord blood to be taken only after delayed cord clamping, Adhere to standardized blood volume draws as per the Ethics committees or SAHPRA CTC review, Infant follow-up should be with qualified personnel and Appropriate emergency trolley as per SAHPRA guidelines must be available on site Sites and Investigators 3.7.1 Clinical trial sites should have investigators who

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: after delayed cord clamping, Adhere to standardized blood volume draws as per the Ethics committees or SAHPRA CTC review, Infant follow-up should be with qualified personnel and Appropriate emergency trolley as per SAHPRA guidelines must be available on site Sites and Investigators 3.7.1 Clinical trial sites should have investigators who are obstetricians/ diplomates or proficient in the management of obstetric emergencies. Sites should be set up to manage these or have quick and established access to a facility with expertise and capacity to manage such outcomes. 3.7.2 Sonography has become an integral part of the standard of antenatal carehence demonstrated experience and/or qualification needs to be provided in the CTF1 Section 2.4. 3.7.3 The inclusion of neonatologists and/or paediatricians should be considered where appropriate in the continuum of care. 3.7.4 Any study that involves pregnant women needs to have a formal SOP on where and how deliveries will be managed. The applicant should propose and justify, based on the complexities of the study, whether incorporation of an obstetrician and /or paediatrician and neonatologist may be necessary. Registration of Investigational Product SAHPRA CTC will only consider pregnancy/lactation-related studies where there is a potential benefit to the South African population. Foetal/ Neonatal and Infant extension 3.9.1 Many studies in pregnancy and lactation may have objectives and endpoints (or estimands) related to the foetus and neonate or infant. 3.9.2 In studies where there are extensions to monitoring the outcomes of neonates and infants, as incorporated in the study design, these studies should include investigators with experience in paediatrics and/ neonatology and incorporate (both parent/ caregiver) TIE and insurance for the neonate/ infant, as well as clinical care for the duration of the study. 3.10 Pregnancy studies with benefit to the Neonate/ Infant 3.10.1 Pregnancy (or maternal) studies may be justified to have value

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: investigators with experience in paediatrics and/ neonatology and incorporate (both parent/ caregiver) TIE and insurance for the neonate/ infant, as well as clinical care for the duration of the study. 3.10 Pregnancy studies with benefit to the Neonate/ Infant 3.10.1 Pregnancy (or maternal) studies may be justified to have value for maternal outcomes, or maternalfoetal, or maternal-infant outcomes. The Ethics thereof are evolving but advanced, especially as regards vaccine studies in the maternal population. SAHPRA recognizes that IPs are also being evaluated in this population. 3.10.2 SAHPRA CTC encourages the implementation of such studies on CTC review. 3.11 Retention of obstetric and paediatric records In South Africa, child health records should be retained at least until the child's 21st birthday, as legally, minors have until three years after reaching the age of majority to make claims. This applies to various health records, including those related to obstetric care. Additionally, records should generally be kept for at least six years after they become dormant (date of last contact). Records for patients with mental incapacities should be kept for their lifetime. 3.12 Databases for Long term follow up of babies in the trial Databases for long term follow up of babies born to pregnant women on clinical studies should be maintained by the sponsor for a period relevant to the study. LACTATION Breastfeeding Support 4.1.1 It is recognised that breastfeeding support and successful initiation and prolongation of breastfeeding in South Africa require a sustained collaborative effort to improve, as evidenced by the Tshwane declaration in support of breastfeeding (2011). 4.1.2 In the context of clinical studies, investigational products can potentially be present in breastmilk and affect the neonate or infant. It is thus necessary to include studies or initiate studies on drug metabolism and excretion during lactation for infant safety. 4.1.3 Although

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: Tshwane declaration in support of breastfeeding (2011). 4.1.2 In the context of clinical studies, investigational products can potentially be present in breastmilk and affect the neonate or infant. It is thus necessary to include studies or initiate studies on drug metabolism and excretion during lactation for infant safety. 4.1.3 Although it is accepted that “breast is best”, outcomes of lactation research may indicate that, in certain circumstances, alternatives to breastfeeding might be an option to avoid exposure to drugs in breastmilk. 4.1.4 Infrastructural support is strongly recommended by providing safe, private spaces at clinical trial centers with lactation consultant support if needed. Cultural/ Religious and Traditional practices and beliefs must be considered in the design of lactation studies. 4.1.5 If required, the inclusion of paediatricians and lactation consultants may be necessary. 4.1.6 Lactation studies in South Africa and other LMICs should be supported Objectives Ultimately, clinical guidance on drug concentrations in breastmilk is driven by 3 outcomes: The concentration of the IP in breastmilk The dose of exposure to the infant The safety (and possibly benefit) to the infant Breastmilk is a dynamic human tissue. Characteristics differ from colostrum to foremilk, hindmilk, premature, and term milk, with intraday variations. Thus, it is recommended that protocol norms be established for uniformity in the collection of specimens. Inclusion of lactating mothers in studies Non-nursing mothers who are still producing breastmilk (but not breastfeeding their infant) may be included in lactation studies. Mothers who are breastfeeding: To assess drug exposure in breastmilk and breastfed infants. Extension of pregnancy studies to the lactation period. Temporary cessation of breastfeeding and replacement with formula will not be allowed. Safety and Efficacy monitoring 4.4.1 The same principles apply with respect to the safety monitoring of lactating mothers and their infants. The table of visit schedules should adequately

title: GUIDELINES TO CLINICAL TRIALS IN PREGNANCY AND
text: breastfed infants. Extension of pregnancy studies to the lactation period. Temporary cessation of breastfeeding and replacement with formula will not be allowed. Safety and Efficacy monitoring 4.4.1 The same principles apply with respect to the safety monitoring of lactating mothers and their infants. The table of visit schedules should adequately consider this in the protocol. 4.4.2 In addition, certain conditions unique to the neonatal period may require extra consideration (growth, development, neonatal pathology). 4.4.3 Neurodevelopmental outcomes may be of consideration for long-term follow-up. 4.4.4 For studies where there is maternal intervention for infant benefit, such as vaccine studies, more information may be obtained by analysis of breastmilk. 4.4.5 Causality with SAEs/ AEs/ AESIs must be interpreted within the context of plausible exposure to IP. 4.4.6 Termination of studies in lactation will be guided by Safety Review committees, DSMBs, and regulatory authorities. Breastmilk Volumes 4.5.1 Standardized reference values for volumes of breastmilk collection in clinical studies are not available. 4.5.2 The minimum amount of breastmilk for the indicated study should be utilized for optimal PK/ PD analysis, or any other analysis. 4.5.3 Breastmilk is considered Human Tissue in South Africa (National Health Act 61 of 2003), and all biological hazard precautions in acquisition, processing, storage, and transport should be taken. An export licence and material transfer agreement will be necessary for the export of the specimen. NOTE: Only a maximum sample storage of 15 years is allowed unless it is scientifically justified. INTRODUCTION Pre-clinical Testing Information from pre-clinical testing is essential in planning clinical trials in humans. For first-in-human (FIH) trials, the information is used to decide what the starting dose should be, and the range of doses to be tested. It also suggests what clinical signs and symptoms as well as laboratory abnormalities should be looked for to detect any adverse effects, especially Serious Adverse Events (SAEs). This document is intended to guide the type and extent of pre-clinical data to be provided in the Clinical Trial Application Form (CTF-1) for submission to SAHPRA for the conduct of a clinical trial in South Africa. Detailed data must be provided in the Investigator’s Brochure and cross-referenced from the CTF-1 where appropriate. In the CTF-1, the applicant is required to provide a summary of the pre-clinical testing that has been conducted during the development of a candidate medicinal or relevant related health products, and a discussion of how this supports the design of the clinical trial in the application. Pre-clinical testing may include both in vitro (laboratory), in silico (computer) and in vivo (animal) studies. The

Pre-clinical testing may include both in vitro (laboratory), in silico (computer) and in vivo (animal) studies. The Guideline is adopted from ICH M3 (R2) non-clinical safety studies for the conduct of human clinical trials for pharmaceuticals - Scientific guideline2. SAHPRA supports the current international principles of the 3Rs - Reduction, Refinement, and Replacement – in animal testing, which involves animal pain, suffering, and/or death. However, in the development of new medicines certain animal tests remain essential for ensuring human safety before clinical investigation. Pre-clinical tests results supporting product functions and safety profile are particularly relevant to support FIH clinical trials but are also important support for subsequent and more extensive clinical trials where physiological or adverse effects observed in animal models can be important for the design of safety surveillance during later phases of clinical development. Pre-clinical test results can provide a preliminary assessment of the balance of risks versus potential benefits of the candidate investigational product (IP). 2 [https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/ich-m3-r2-non-clinical-safety-studies-conduct-human-clinical-trials-pharmaceuticalsscientific-guideline] Animal testing can be used for elucidation of biodistribution, metabolism and elimination and evaluation of the investigational product activity if a suitable animal model is available. Animal models should be validated and appropriate for the class of medicine/device being tested. Small-animal models, including mice and rats, may be useful for toxicity testing, but larger animal species are more appropriate for investigating physiological functions and may include rabbits, dogs, sheep, pigs and nonhuman primates. Toxicity testing of pharmaceutical medicines should establish a No-Observed-Adverse-Effect-Level (NOAEL) in an appropriate animal model and may be determined during repeat dose toxicity studies. Pre-clinical testing of medical devices is necessary to establish safety

text: more appropriate for investigating physiological functions and may include rabbits, dogs, sheep, pigs and nonhuman primates. Toxicity testing of pharmaceutical medicines should establish a No-Observed-Adverse-Effect-Level (NOAEL) in an appropriate animal model and may be determined during repeat dose toxicity studies. Pre-clinical testing of medical devices is necessary to establish safety and functional capabilities. Where animal models are needed, they must be qualified as appropriate for establishment of the required endpoint that maybe anatomical or physiological. In addition, for Biosimilar medicines, the investigational product must be fully characterised by comparative physico-chemical testing, demonstration of functional activity (e.g., receptor binding in cell cultures), and in vivo testing as “Biosimilar3” before it can be included in clinical trials. SAHPRA may consider that for biosimilar medicines, established by comparative physico-chemical and functional similarity studies, in-vivo testing may be unnecessary. Clinical Factors in early Clinical Trials The Clinical factors section outlines the key clinical considerations relevant to dose selection, dose escalation, maximum exposure, and transition between single and multiple dosing regimens, with particular emphasis on healthy volunteer studies. It also addresses the planning and conduct of early clinical trials, including protocol design, participant selection, safety monitoring, data review, stopping rules, and communication of adverse events. In addition, the responsibilities of sponsors and investigators, as well as requirements for clinical site facilities and emergency preparedness, are described. Collectively, these principles aim to support informed decision-making, minimize risk, and ensure regulatory compliance throughout the early stages of clinical development. CLINICAL FACTORS: CONSIDERATIONS FOR PHASE-I/FIH CLINICAL TRIALS 7.1 Dose selection for FIH and early clinical trials The starting dose and maximum exposure, as well as dose escalation steps during the clinical trial, should be justified and outlined in the protocol. The methods used and calculations on how doses and estimated exposure levels were determined, including methods for modelling (e.g., PK/PD and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK)), should be summarised in the CTF-1 and protocol and the details included in the investigational brochure (IB). Deviations from the prespecified dose escalation and decision-making criteria would warrant

Deviations from the prespecified dose escalation and decision-making criteria would warrant the submission of substantial amendment(s). Decision making criteria for adapting dosage based on clinical data based on emerging clinical data should be described. In addition, sentinel dosing of two participants (one active, one placebo) is required at a minimum for the first single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple ascending dose (MAD) cohorts. 7.1.1 Starting dose for Healthy Volunteers Sentinel safety cohorts are small groups of participants dosed before the main cohort. These may help to identify potential adverse effects, and mitigate risk, especially in FIH and Phase 1 trials. The starting dose must mitigate the risk of toxicity while balancing the need to elicit pharmacologic activity. Reference should be made to published guidance documents from EMA and the FDA for investigators to follow when determining an appropriate starting dose. There are two methods that may be used for calculating the starting dose; an empirical or a mechanistic approach. The empirical approach aims at avoiding toxicity at initial human doses by using the NOAEL, a generally accepted benchmark for safety (FDA). The exposures achieved at the NOAEL in the most relevant animal species used (which might not necessarily be the most sensitive species) should be used for the estimation of an equivalent exposure for humans. The mechanistic approach is based on state-of-the-art modelling incorporating all relevant preclinical pharmacology data, including ex vivo and in vitro studies in human tissues (EMA). This approach enables the selection of a minimal anticipated biological effect dose-level, as this is becoming increasingly important as more targeted

text: equivalent exposure for humans. The mechanistic approach is based on state-of-the-art modelling incorporating all relevant preclinical pharmacology data, including ex vivo and in vitro studies in human tissues (EMA). This approach enables the selection of a minimal anticipated biological effect dose-level, as this is becoming increasingly important as more targeted therapies are being developed that are very specific and potent, with predicted pharmacologically active doses well below a dose that is thought to be safe based on the NOAEL. 7.1.2 Maximum Dose Selection The maximum exposure should be justified based on all available pre-clinical and clinical data, including PD, PK, findings in toxicity studies, and exposure at the expected therapeutic dose range. An expected maximum exposure level must not be exceeded in the study without approval of a substantial protocol amendment, this should have been pre-defined in the protocol for each study part. 7.1.3 Moving from single and multiple dosing The selection of an appropriate dosing interval and duration of dosing for all multiple dosing cohorts and study parts should consider the specific PK and PD characteristics of the IP, the available non-clinical safety data, and all data from participants in previous single-dose cohorts. A maximum duration of dosing should be stated in the protocol for every cohort. The expected exposure after multiple dosing (Cmax and AUC 0-tau) should have been covered during preceding SAD parts/trials. 7.1.4 Route of Administration The choice of route of administration for dosing in humans should be based on the pre-clinical data, the characteristics of the IP, and the intended therapeutic use. 7.2 Planning and conducting early clinical trials 7.2.1 Protocol - Overall design The following are key considerations: a) Description of the trial and its ethical and scientific rationale. This would Include a description of what is being done in the trial and the rationale behind key decisions so that the trial can be subject to scrutiny in regulatory assessment. b) Graphical representation of the overall scheme of the proposed trial in real-time, showing intervals for interventions, sampling, timing of all reviews, and decision points. c) Details on the size of the cohorts, including how many participants are on active IP and how many are on placebo treatment. d) Phase-1 clinical trials typically enroll small groups of participants; about 20 per cohort, and less than 100 for the whole trial. 7.2.2 Integrated protocol The practice of conducting FIH/early clinical trials with integrated protocols means that the information generated in previous parts needs to be analysed and integrated into an assessment in a limited timeframe before deciding on proceeding to the next part. All parts, and the criteria to move from one part to another, should be predefined within an integrated protocol, as should possible modifications, based on the totality of available information and the related uncertainty. Recommendations for time sequence for the conduct of different parts: a) Overlapping of SAD and MAD parts may be acceptable. The proposed overlap, however, should be scientifically justified and supported by decision points and a review of available data before starting the MAD part. b) Other single-dose parts (e.g., food interaction) could be conducted in parallel to the SAD part, provided the dose chosen and the expected exposure are equal to or lower than that which was reached in a concluded preceding SAD cohort where all relevant data

text: data before starting the MAD part. b) Other single-dose parts (e.g., food interaction) could be conducted in parallel to the SAD part, provided the dose chosen and the expected exposure are equal to or lower than that which was reached in a concluded preceding SAD cohort where all relevant data have been reviewed and no dose escalation stopping criteria were met. c) Other study parts that involve multiple dosing (e.g., drug-drug interaction) should generally not overlap with earlier SAD or MAD cohorts. All relevant SAD and MAD data should be reviewed before starting these parts. Deviation from this should be justified in the protocol. 7.2.3 Choice of participants The choice to conduct FIH trials in healthy participants or patients should be made on a case‐by‐case basis. The risks of enrolling healthy volunteers versus patients must be weighed, including toxicities, PK variability, lifestyle conditions, benefits to patients, and special populations. Clinical factors to consider in the decision to conduct a study in healthy volunteers or patients include: a) Whether the toxicities foreseen/risks associated can support the inclusion of healthy volunteers. b) The relative presence of the molecular target in healthy participants or in patients. c) The possible variable PK, PD or safety profile in participants. d) The potential differences between the targeted patient group and healthy volunteers. e) Possible interactions with participants’ lifestyle, e.g., smoking, use of alcohol or recreational drugs. f) The use of other medications with the possibility of adverse reactions and/or difficulties in the interpretation of results. g) A potential of patients to benefit from other products or interventions. h) The predicted therapeutic window of the IP based on preclinical testing. i) Factors relating to special populations, including age, gender, ethnicity, and genotype(s). Key inclusion and exclusion criteria for trials involving healthy participants should include an adequate set

Key inclusion and exclusion criteria for trials involving healthy participants should include an adequate set of vital signs (including ECG), laboratory values and clinical assessments that should be within normal ranges. A justification for deviations outside the defined normal ranges should be provided. 7.2.4 Safety monitoring and interventions The detection of a safety signal with a high degree of certainty is extremely limited by the typically small size of these trials. Successful signal detection in FIH studies depends on adequate collection of data coupled to a systematic analysis of the data, a determination of the strength of a potential signal, and an understanding of the quantitative limitations of typical study designs. The participant’s safety assessments that will be routinely conducted, their timing, and any additional monitoring actions or interventions should be pre-specified in line with the known pharmacological and nonclinical safety profile and balanced against the degree of uncertainty. Any proposal to routinely omit an assessment should be scientifically based. The length of follow-up of participants should be specified within the protocol (e.g., for possible delayed adverse reactions). The sponsor should describe how safety monitoring should be extended until parameters return to within the normal range or to baseline, as appropriate for the population. Extended monitoring should be considered, e.g., when the mechanism entails enzyme inhibition or activation (monitoring should continue until enzyme activity has returned to baseline or to an acceptable percentage of baseline) or when prolonged PD effects are observed, regardless of duration of target inhibition or the PK profile of the IP. Repeated assessments, integrating available knowledge with rapid processing of emerging information, are crucial for the recognition of developing toxicity at an early stage. 7.2.5 Data review for decisions The data supporting dose escalation or the beginning of a new study part in alignment with the predefined criteria in the protocol are key and should be described in the protocol. The following are regarded as minimum criteria for data review: • Evaluation of data by a defined expert group and summary of criteria for evaluation and progression to the next dose-level. • ‘Evaluable’ participants should be defined, i.e., participants who have completed all planned study visits at least until the time of the decision as detailed in the protocol. • Data collection as planned in the protocol in each dosing cohort should be complete and the decision to proceed to the next dose cohort should be documented. 7.2.6 Early Stopping rules The protocol should define unambiguous stopping rules that result in an immediate stop to dosing. Stopping rules should be defined for each of the following: • Final stop to dosing and termination of the trial; • Stopping for an individual participant, at any time in the trial; • Stopping within a cohort − when participants in a cohort are dosed staggered; − during multiple dosing; • Progression to the next part of the trial; • Any dose escalation parts of the trial. Consideration should be given to the inclusion of independent experts who are (at least) external to the study. ETHICS AND REGULATORY FACTORS: 10.1 Role of RECS and the NHREC: Due to their inherently high-risk nature, Phase I studies, parƟcularly ﬁrst-in-human trials (FIHs), also require heightened atenƟon from Health Research Ethics Commitees (RECs). In most phase 1 / FIH studies with healthy volunteer parƟcipants, reviewers need to balance the potenƟal risk of harm with possible future beneﬁts to the general community, while in the case of oncology and gene therapy studies, reviewers need to balance the risk of harm with any potenƟal beneﬁts to the both the parƟcipant and to the general community. Special atenƟon should be given to preclinical data, dose selecƟon and escalaƟon, safety monitoring plans, stopping rules, parƟcipant selecƟon criteria, and the adequacy of informed consent processes. In the case of oncology and gene therapy studies, addiƟonal atenƟon should be given to the underlying disease process and comorbidiƟes of the study parƟcipants. In addiƟon, when reviewing such studies, the REC reviewers must parƟcularly follow both the latest SAGCP Guidelines and the NaƟonal Department of Health (NDoH) Ethics in Research Guidelines, developed by the NaƟonal Health Research Ethics Council (NHREC). Through this structured oversight framework, RECs and the NHREC play a criƟcal role in ensuring that earlyphase clinical research in South Africa is conducted ethically, responsibly, and in a manner that protects parƟcipant safety while advancing scienƟﬁc knowledge. 10.2 Other Regulatory AuthoriƟes: When reviewing Phase I and especially FIHs in South Africa, informaƟon used and decisions made, parƟcularly concerning the risk of harm, made by other Regulatory AuthoriƟes

title: This document is intended to provide guidance to applicants on the scheduling of substances submitted for registration as medicines.
text: This document is intended to provide guidance to applicants on the scheduling of substances submitted for registration as medicines. It represents the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority’s current thinking on the safety, quality and efficacy of medicines and takes into account the country’s obligations in terms of international agreements. It is not intended as an exclusive approach. The Authority reserves the right to request any additional information to establish the scheduling status of a medicine in keeping with the knowledge current at the time of evaluation. Alternative approaches may be used but these should be scientifically and technically justified. It is important that applicants adhere to the administrative requirements to avoid delays in the processing and evaluation of applications. Document History Final Version Reason for Amendment Effective Date First issue 30 May 2022 Alignment to the latest SAHPRA guideline template Introduction to the Rescheduling Application Form and general process alignments. DR BOITUMELO SEMETE-MAKOKOTLELA CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER Glossary Abbreviation/ Term Meaning API Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient SAHPRA South Arican Health Products Regulatory Authority 1. INTRODUCTION This guideline is intended to provide applicants, Holders of Certificates of Registration (HCR) with guidance on the criteria applied by the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (“SAHPRA” or “the Authority”) when applying for the rescheduling of a medicine or substance. Purpose This purpose of this document is to provide guidance to applicants on the rescheduling of registered medicinal products. Scope This Guideline contains guidance on the suitability of rescheduling medicines or substances. This guideline should be read in conjunction with the Medicines and Related Substances Act, 1965 (Act 101 of 1965) (herein referred to as the Medicines Act), as amended, and the Regulations issued in terms of this Act; and the latest version of the Consolidated Schedules. 2. LEGAL PROVISION In terms of the Medicines Act, a ‘Scheduled substance’ is defined as follows: “means any medicine or other substance prescribed by the Minister under section 22A”. Section 22A(2) empowers the Minister of Health “on the recommendation of SAHPRA”, to make the Schedules referred to in that section, Section 37A also empowers the Minister, again on the recommendation of SAHPRA, to amend the Schedules by notice in the Government Gazette. The official Schedules shall therefore always be those that have been published in the Government Gazette or amended by subsequent notice in the Gazette. All medicines are subject to a scheduling process on the basis of the substances (active pharmaceutical ingredients) they contain. The primary consideration in scheduling a substance is its safety profile, in relation to the therapeutic indications for its use. Substances may be listed in one or more of eight Schedules. However, substances may also be listed in more than one Schedule, based on dosage form, route of administration, strength, indication, dose, duration of treatment or a combination of these factors. Where a substance or medicine has been listed in more than one Schedule, the other Schedule(s) in which it is listed is/ are indicated in parentheses after the inscription in a particular Schedule. Where exceptions are included in an entry, these have been emphasised by printing the word ―except in bold type. 3. GENERAL INFORMATION The application form for Rescheduling of a Substance or Medicine (GLF-CEM-NS-01A) is to be used for applications regarding rescheduling of a substance or medicine in line with the Guideline to the Scheduling of Substances and Medicines (SAHPGL-CEM-NS-02). The application form can be accessible on SAHPRA website. An application can be submitted by an applicant who wishes to change the schedule status of a registered medicine. An independent person/s or association may not apply for a rescheduling of a product. However, the independent persons or association may bring forth data/ information to the regulator to highlight any safety/ efficacy concerns observed by the persons or association for the regulator to assess if a feasible action is required. NOTE: Safety and efficacy data concerns may be submitted to the regulator independently, where applicable. The same principles as outlined in the Guideline to the Scheduling of Substances and Medicines (SAHPGL-CEM-NS-02) would be applied in considering an application for rescheduling. Therefore, to justify rescheduling from Schedule 3 or 4 to Schedule 2 or 1, evidence would need to be provided to justify use without a prescription. If any of the following criteria are met, prescription status would need to be maintained: The substance is likely to present a direct or indirect danger to human health, even when used correctly, if used without supervision by a medical practitioner or dentist; The substance is frequently and to a very wide extent used incorrectly or inappropriately, and as a result is likely to present a direct or indirect danger to human health; The safety and efficacy of the substance has not yet been adequately described and requires further investigation. Likewise, in order to justify

Likewise, in order to justify a Schedule 0 status, evidence would need to be provided to show that the hazard to health, the risk of misuse and the need for special precautions in handling are minimal, and that wider sale would be a convenience to the consumer. A product is normally assigned the highest scheduling status appropriate to any one of the registered indications of the product. If an application is made to reschedule only selected indications of a specific product to a lower Schedule a unique name and a separate registration dossier, where applicable, will be required for such a product. It must be noted that dual scheduling on packaging, Professional Information and the Patient Information Leaflet is not permitted. Only products with indications, strengths, routes of administration and/ or pack sizes applicable to the lower schedule will qualify for the lower scheduling status. 4.
